items.body: The latest installment in the Portraits GRM series pairs the duo of crys cole & Oren Ambarchi with Italian maestro Giuseppe Ielasi. Each occupying a full side of vinyl, the result is a document of where contemporary sound practice finds itself in 2026 while paying homage to the institutional framework that made such work possible. This is not musique concrète in the traditional sense, but it is undeniably born from the same spirit of inquiry that drove Pierre Schaeffer to upend our relationship with sound nearly eighty years ago. Pierre Schaeffer (1910-1995) is remembered not necessarily for his music, or even his philosophical contributions to the study of sound (which were significant), but for his institution building. After pioneering musique concrète while working in French radio in the late 1940s and early 1950s, Schaeffer began almost instantly institutionalizing his legacy, what became the Groupe de Recherches Musicales (GRM) in 1958 (known as Ina-GRM since 1975). The tension between preserving a tradition and remaining open to the new has defined the institution ever since. My 2019 interview with François J. Bonnet—composer, philosopher, and current director of Ina-GRM—explored precisely this question: how does an institution honor its past while making space for the unfamiliar? An answer arrived in 2020 with the launch of Portraits GRM, a series of commissioned releases designed to bring contemporary voices into the GRM’s hallowed studios. The first release was Jim O’Rourke’s Shutting Down Here, fittingly so, as his sessions there spanned 30 years and thus that work’s completion constituted the closing of a significant loop. The re-issuing of classic and adjacent GRM titles began under the direction of Editions Mego, but after the death of Peter Rehberg (Pita) in 2021, the series transitioned to the stewardship of Shelter Press. Since then, Portraits GRM has featured Lucy Railton, Okkyung Lee, Kali Malone, Lasse Marhaug, Laurel Halo, Beatrice Dillon, and many others—artists who share little aesthetically but are united by a willingness to push against the boundaries of what sound can do. As with most installments in the series, the latest release offers two compelling sidelong works from heavyweights of the experimental underground. On one side, crys cole and Oren Ambarchi continue their collaborative exploration of texture and density; on the other, Giuseppe Ielasi presents something distinctly his own. crys cole & Oren Ambarchi ~ Sparkling or Silent The title suggests something binary—a flickering between presence and absence, articulation and withholding—but the piece itself operates in the spaces between. Sparkling or Silent opens with what might best be described as ASMR-concrète: close-mic’d rustling, breath, the micro-articulations of objects manipulated in near-silence. It is intimate yet abstract, as though the listener has stumbled upon a private ritual. Over its 19’43’’ duration, the work unfolds in several distinct movements, each building upon the last until the accumulated density becomes something else entirely. Oren Ambarchi needs little introduction. The Australian guitarist has built a formidable reputation as a solo artist and one of the most prolific collaborators in experimental music, with a discography that touches on everything from the glacial drone of his solo work to the rhythmic propulsion of his trio with Johan Berthling and Andreas Werliin—whose Ghosted series has only grown more assured with each installment. Records including Grapes from the estate (2004), Hubris (2016), and Simian Angel (2019) are personal favorites, not to mention his ongoing dialogues with figures like Keiji Haino and Jim O’Rourke. But alongside this celebrated career, there exists another body of work, equally significant if less discussed: his partnership with crys cole. Likely the less familiar name to many listeners, cole’s work is no less deserving of attention. I have been a fan of this Canadian sound artist’s practice for years, both in her solo work and her collaborations. Her third album for Black Truffle, Making Conversation collects three recent commissioned pieces and demonstrates a trajectory that has moved steadily toward greater formal control without sacrificing the tactile, almost sculptural quality of her sound. She had been involved with Winnipeg’s send + receive festival for over a decade, contributed photographs and projections to classic Canadian experimental records, and continues to be an active performer and sound artist. Her work with Ora Clementi—the duo with James Rushford—offers a dense thicket of sonic material that feels both organic and constructed. Sylva Sylvarum, in particular, stands as a high-water mark in her collaborative output. On Ambarchi’s Audience of One (2012), she’s credited as contributing contact microphones and brushes to the track “Passage.” They’ve since produced several records as a duo: Sonja Henies Vei 31 (2014), a hazy collage of intimate gesture and field recordings from a Norwegian sojourn; Hotel Record (2017), its title a dryly witty reference to its origins in hotel room sessions, a study in digital textures; and Gallivant (2021), documenting a live concert from the previous year. The pair have often played with others, including Keith Rowe and Leif Elggren. The collaborative dynamic is worth dwelling on, if only because there is something peculiar and generative about a musical duo that is also a romantic couple. One thinks of the historical precedents: Sonny and Linda Sharrock, whose volatile partnership produced some of the most ferocious free jazz of the late 1960s and early 1970s; Max Roach and Abby Lincoln, whose work together addressed civil rights with a moral urgency that still resonates, again overshadowed by a documented history of abuse. More recently, and hopefully less problematically, I think of Christina Vantzou and John Also Bennett, Matmos (MC Schmidt and Drew Daniel), and Two-Way Street—Ashlee Booth on cello and Adam Lion on percussion, for whom Sarah Hennies wrote a piece exploring precicely the dynamic between a romantic and musical partnership. Giuseppe Ielasi and Jennifer Veillerobe have even released a few short pieces as Eselsohr. There is something about the intimacy of shared life that translates into the shared space of improvisation and composition, a trust that allows for risk without the safety net of distance. A residency abroad, a portrait of two artists developing a shared vocabulary in confined spaces, the energy of a live recording. Sparkling or Silent represents something different—a consciously composed concert work. As the Portraits GRM materials describe it, the piece is “a moment apart in their respective artistic approaches” where an electroacoustic method that has always been latent in both of their practices “here asserts itself as a central compositional modality.” This shift from documentation to composition makes Sparkling or Silent feel more expansive and considered, even if it doesn’t necessarily represent a linear “evolution” so much as a deliberate side-step into a different mode of working. From its intimate opening, Sparkling or Silent gradually accumulates tonal densisty before dissolving again. About halfway through, after cohering into a sustained drone cloud, the texture thins; ghostly melodies and gentle rustlings emerge from the haze, while field recordings slowly ground us in an unexpected place. The real surprise arrives in the final four minutes: a sudden chorus of truck (?) horn harmonies. The effect recalls Alvin Curran’s Maritime Rites, transposed from water to asphalt; the collective ritual of Curran’s foghorns replaced by the found sounds of the highway. Within a minute, these sounds accumulate into a dense, surprisingly consonant cluster, overlapping blares forming a sustained fog of noise that continues until, finally, the sparkle turns to silence. It is a closing gesture that reframes everything that came before, revealing the delicate rustlings of the opening as part of a larger soundscape that extends far beyond the studio walls. The piece does not so much end as disperse, its constituent parts returning to the world from which they were borrowed.   Giuseppe Ielasi ~ unfamiliar music (paris) In Milano in 2017, I met Giuseppe Ielasi and Jennifer Veillerobe for dinner accompanied by Oren and crys, who were part-time residents of the city then—their European headquarters, before relocating to Berlin, was this underrated Italian metropolis, a base between their Australian and Canadian homelands. So in my mind, the connection between the artists featured on this record is obvious, forged not only through shared aesthetics but through shared meals, shared cities, shared lives. But Ielasi’s relationship to this series extends far beyond personal connections. He has mastered every Portraits GRM record except the first, and his own Senufo label released early records by Kassel Jaeger, which was in fact my introduction to François J. Bonnet many years ago. This record, then, feels like a culmination; the current director of Ina-GRM, the mastering engineer, the series, and the artists all intertwined in a web of mutual influence and respect that spans decades. Ielasi’s catalog is deep and varied, marked by a restless curiosity that refuses to settle into comfortable routines. He has his interests and proclivities—a fascination with small sounds, repetition, motors, unusual rhythmic grooves, in other words “an insistence on material”—but he rarely deploys the same technical setup or approach twice, constantly searching for new means of expression. This commitment to renewal is evident throughout his discography, from his early work on the 12k label to his more recent return to explorations of guitar and electronics. unfamiliar music (paris) arrives with some precedent. Ielasi has performed at the GRM before; I have a recording from 20 January 2014 at GRM Paris that captures his take on acousmatic diffusion. The title itself is shared with unfamiliar music vol.1 (guitar duets), a 2024 digital record that expanded a renewed focus on guitar as a sound source that began with releases in 2020. But what connection does this new piece have to that earlier work? The title seems to refer less to a specific genre or instrumentation and more to a mode of production, an approach to working with sound that prioritizes the strange, the dislocated, the not-quite-familiar. The cover of this release depicts Ielasi performing in Paris with a sampler, suggesting a process rooted in improvisation and constraint. And indeed, some of the samples in the piece do seem to be shared with previously released works, here recontextualized and repurposed. This is not a work of pure creation ex nihilo but of rearrangement, of finding new relationships between existing materials, a practice that echoes both the concrète tradition as well as Ielasi’s own history of pushing it into new territory. The GRM’s acousmatic tradition is evident in the microphone technique and in the spatial treatment of sounds, but there is also a digital air to the proceedings that feels distinctly contemporary, a reminder that the techniques Schaeffer pioneered have been absorbed, transformed, and rendered nearly invisible in the work of subsequent generations. Where cole and Ambarchi’s contribution moves from intimacy to surreal mundanity, Ielasi’s work operates in a different register entirely. The piece itself unfolds as a study in gentle contrast and rhythmic accumulation. The rhythmic elements that have long characterized his work are present but transformed—pulses that never quite lock into a predictable groove, small sounds that build into larger textures, a sense of propulsion that constantly threatens to derail itself. Static gives way to layers of competing rhythm gives way to a mobile lullaby. unfamiliar music (paris) passes through a range of sonic territories without any clear delineations between movements. Ielasi opts instead for a gradual process of substitution. What emerges is a piece that feels both of its moment and somehow outside of it. The “unfamiliar” of the title is not a description of the sounds themselves but of the relationships between them, the way they refuse to settle into expected patterns or resolve into comfortable listening. Ielasi makes music that demands attention without demanding understanding, that rewards close listening without promising easy rewards.   Taken together with the cole and Ambarchi piece, this release offers a portrait of the series at its best: two works that share little in common but are united by a willingness to push against the boundaries of what sound can do, and a commitment to the kind of exploration that Schaeffer himself would have recognized. The Portraits GRM series continues to honor its institutional legacy not through preservation but through renewal, not by looking backward but by making space for the unfamiliar. (Joseph Sannicandro)
items._cn_summary: Portraits GRM系列最新一期将crys cole与Oren Ambarchi的合作与Giuseppe Ielasi的独奏分别置于黑胶唱片两面，是对当代声音实践现状的一份文献式记录，同时向孕育这些作品的机构传统致敬。crys cole与Ambarchi延续他们对质感和密度的探索，作品《Sparkling or Silent》以近距离拾音的窸窣、呼吸与物体的微声开篇，营造亲密而抽象的聆听体验，如同偶然撞见一场私密仪式，全长近二十分钟，分为数个清晰段落。Ielasi则呈现独具个人语汇的另一面作品。该系列由Editions Mego转至Shelter Press发行后，已邀请Lucy Railton、Kali Malone、Beatrice Dillon等众多实验音乐人参与，他们在美学上各异，却共同致力于拓展声音的边界。

items.body: As I already had the privilege to write a feature about the posthumously released album Stellar Regions on this blog, i want to stretch this even a bit further. Here, I take a look at the period to follow, which eventually and fatally turned out to be the last five months in John Coltrane’s life. My focus is on the production of music in this final stage, as far it has been recorded and released, rather than John’s personal or health condition. On 15 February 1967, John had recorded the tracks eventually released as Stellar Regions in 1995 (see my earlier feature) with the quartet. One week later, on 22 February 1967, he returned with Rashied Ali for a saxophone – drums duo session, eventually to be released as Interstellar Space (see Gary Chapin‘s feature on this album). On 07 March 1967, in another session with the quartet again, he recorded two tracks, as far as we know, Ogunde and Number One . Ogunde is, first of all, a relatively short piece at a few seconds over 3 ½ minutes. A noticeable parallel to Stellar Regions , where the title track and Iris have approximately the same length and concise structure. The track takes its title presumably from an afro-brazilean folk song „Ogundu Varere“, rougly translated as a prayer to the gods. John occupied himself with spiritual traditions especially from Africa. John uses his forceful, cry-like late saxophone sound, overblowing his instrument, which gives an emotional urgence to the piece. The theme starts with a solemn, hmyn-like melody, but breaks out in free, atonal outbursts, before it fades away. In summary, John condenses the intensity of his (at that time) usually half-hour long live improvisations into less than a handful of minutes (but see below, what happened live). At some time in spring (David S. Wild confirmed in the liner notes for Stellar Regions that this track was not recorded on 15 February, so the actual recording date remains unknown), John must have recorded To Be , where he plays flute and is rejoined by Pharoah Sanders on piccolo flute. He shows a very calm, introspective and meditative side here. At over 16 minutes playing time, this track feels like a spiritual retreat. The two flutes give it an airy, almost floating mood. Alice Coltrane’s flowing piano style provides a mystic, harp-like cushion. Rashied Ali on drums and Jimmy Garrison on bass keep it calm and subdued. All together, the piece lacks a trditional jazz pulse, even leaves traditional jazz structures completely and makes a profound structural switch towards a meditative, open-end spiritual incantation. It stands as one of the most explicit artifacts of the creative partnership between John and Alice at that final stage and already mirrors the „cosmic jazz“ landscapes that Alice would pioneer on her own in the years to follow in her landmark solo releases ( Universal Consciousness , Journey in Satchidananda). Not to forget about Pharoah Sanders (Karma). Also unknown is the exact recording date for the piece titled Expression in spring 1967 with the quartet, which later lended its title to the album. 23 April 1967 is the date of the last live recording, The Olatunji Concert. This performance, originally recorded for a radio broadcast, is featured by Fotis Nikolakopoulos on this blog, so see there. With due respect to Fotis, I will limit myself here to the absolutely striking contrast between the live version of Ogunde and the studio version. Performed live, it swells to 28 minutes playing time. The studio recording’s tight and condensed structure is only preserved in the theme at the beginning to which it returns only at the very end. In between, it gets overwhelmed by a storm-like wave of pure energy. After the introduction of the melody as theme, the structure collapses completely in a ritual storm. A dense, polyrhythmic vortex is unchained in Rashied Ali’s drumming. Alice Coltrane plays cascade-like runs on the piano. On saxophone, Pharoah Sanders adds his bone-rattling, ecstatic overblowing cries. Yes, the quartet has been expanded here. Pharoah Sanders is back at it on the second saxophone. Two additional percussionists joined in, Algie DeWitt and Jumma Santos. The last ever live gig came at Baltimore’s Famous Ballroom on May 7, 1967. No audio recording of that performance is known to exist. On 17 May 1967, exactly two months before John’s death, a sextet met for a last studio recording. The master tapes have been lost or at least unissued so two tracks with the titles None Other and Kaleidoscope have been unreleased so far and do not even appear on retrospective compilations. With the recorded material, a last studio record was conceived during John’s lifetime. It was given the title Expression . John was actively involved in the production and met with Bob Thiele. On side 1, it had Ogunde as the opening track (the studio version, as above, of course). Track #2 was To Be with John and Pharoah Sanders on flutes (as above). At over 16 minutes, it was the longest track, making up for nearly half of the original album’s playing time, and the only track on the album in which Pharoah Sanders made an appearance. Side 2 opened with the majestic ballad Offering , the only track chosen from the 15 February session, thus making it the only track on the posthumous album Stellar Regions (see there) that had been released before and had an original title. Hank Shteamer has just featured this track prominently in the New York Times and put it into the larger context of spiritual jazz, for which a piece like Offering „would seem like a perfect prototype“ (Hank Shteamer, Spiritual Jazz Has Turned Cozy. John Coltrane Demanded More. New York Times, September 18, 2026). The original album closed with the title track Expression, John‘s last studio recording to ever be released. In the later CD release only, Number O ne, recorded on the same day as Ogunde , was added as a bonus track (the track, however, had been released for the first time in a 1978 compilation album). Obviously, the most recent recording session of May 1967 was not considered in the process at all (at that time, the tapes at least should still have been around, I guess?). John reportedly selected the four tracks for the original album release and their exact sequence himself. On Friday, 14 July 1967, three days before his death, he met Bob Thiele, handed the master tapes over to him and finally authorised the title and the release of the album, but expressed his opposition against liner notes. Expression , as John Coltrane’s final statement, was released in September 1967, two months after his death, containing John‘s chronologically last audible studio recordings and being the first posthumous release of his music. items._cn_summary: 文章梳理了约翰·科特兰去世前五个月内留下的录音创作，包括与四重奏及鼓手拉希德·阿里合作的唱片。评论重点分析《Ogunde》：短篇作品以祈求为主题，萨克斯运用强力度、近乎哭喊的音色与过吹技巧，压缩了现场即兴的强度。《To Be》则转向长笛与短笛的冥想表达，爱丽丝·科特兰的钢琴如竖琴般铺陈，几乎脱离传统爵士节拍，呈现开放的灵性吟唱。文章也指出其与非洲、巴西传统及爱丽丝日后宇宙爵士创作之间的联系。

items.body: Over the past five years, Philip Samartzis has been building a body of distinct work. The interrelated recordings are identifiable by their adjacent titles: 2021’s Polar Force / Array (with Eugene Ughetti); 2023’s Atmospheres and Disturbances; 2024’s Air Pressure (with Michael Vorfeld); and now 2026’s Atmospheric Pressure, again with Vorfeld. The starting point for these ventures was a pair of residencies sponsored by the Australian Antarctic Territory Arts Fellowship program. Samartzis was able to capture some incredible recordings in sub-zero temperatures, and they have proven to be a wealth of material in both pure and sculpted forms. As on Air Pressure, Samartzis contributes electronics, Vorfeld stringed instruments and percussion. The new set zeroes in on a 36-hour blizzard at the Casey Research Station in 2016. Amid the hundred-knot winds and white-out conditions, “the station was reduced to pressure, vibration, and sound.” Simply picturing David Nielson’s cover image of David Ward inspecting dog lines in 1990, one can already feel the cold and intuit the level of difficulty. “Gravitational Overflow” sets the stage with slowly increasing winds and the creak of vanes (personified by Vorfeld’s instruments). The wind and snow create their own music, an undulating drone of literal white noise. Percussion enters as sympathetic partner; one imagines the rattling of glass and iron, caught in a maelstrom of Biblical proportions. Toward the end, these metallic pats and taps take center stage, as if representing the eye of the hurricane. “Depression” refers to atmospheric conditions, although one would be forgiven for thinking that it might mirror a mood. The isolation of research stations often produces feelings of malaise. The electronics and radio chatter are surprises in the wake of the opener; some portions even sound like turntable scratches or graffiti cans being shaken. The focus is not on the machine hum and motor sputter, but instead, what happens when the electricity fails. The purely percussive section arrives earlier, in the sixth minute, like the last sounds of a man caught in a storm, having lost all bearings, facing death by making music one last time, his only audience the abyss. “Cold Front” reveals the full depth of the danger. The strings seem as agitated as the snow, the percussion as frozen as the sleet, the electronics as charged as the air. Sound bends around the cymbals like sheets of ice. In the sixth minute, a sound like clomping hooves comes across like a phantasm. The actual storm mixes with the impression of the storm to convey feelings of being trapped inside or wandering outside: stir crazy or snow-blind. The applause at the very end is well-earned. We’re not sure how many more Antarctic recordings Samartzis has in the bag, but as so few of us are likely to hear them in person, each release arrives as a revelation. (Richard Allen)
items._genre: field recording / drone / ambient / experimental / electroacoustic
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑基于2016年凯西研究站36小时暴风雪的实地录音，由Philip Samartzis负责电子声音处理，Michael Vorfeld贡献弦乐与打击乐。作品将极端环境中的风声、金属撞击与电子噪音融合，营造出白噪音式的波动音场。乐评指出，每首曲目都捕捉了暴风雪不同阶段的听觉质感：开场以缓慢增强的气流与风向标的嘎吱声铺垫；中段通过纯粹打击乐段落呈现孤立感与失控感；终曲则将弦乐与电子声音比作风暴中飘散的冰片，在第六分钟突然出现类似幽灵马蹄声的不安声响。评论认为，这些录音珍贵之处在于大多数人无法亲历南极环境，每张专辑的发布都像一次揭示，将自然力量转化为可聆听的抽象声音艺术。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — It is no coincidence that many electronic music artists draw inspiration from the past, specifically the 1970s. The British duo Boards of Canada creates a sound that feels progressive in an electronic sense, much like the Norwegian duo R�yksopp has done at times. It is the art of layering sounds, not haphazardly, but with a very clear purpose: to evoke moods and suggest mental images or ideas that often transcend mere musical concepts. The cover of their debut album, Music Has the Right to Children, always struck me as very retro, very 1960s, yet upon closer inspection, much like a painting bearing an artist's signature, one discovers that the figures lack actual faces. They are blank slates, leaving the viewer to imagine what lies within. "An Eagle in Your Mind" offers a magnetic groove, featuring a downtempo rhythm with a strong, minimalist trip-hop foundation. The track combines an organic drum feel with the presence of both samples and scratching, making it highly appealing and modern; it also reminds me of another underground classic, Vernon Reid's first solo album, Mistaken Identity (1996), which blended heavy guitar work with electronic elements and featured DJ Logic.Short tracks like "The Color of the Fire" reminded me, in the spaces between the longer pieces, of the intros on Gong's Angel's Egg, as well as the poetic ambient atmospheres of Brian Eno. The use of analog synthesizers also draws a parallel to another electronic duo, the French group Air, and in "Telephasic Workshop," we can observe how two parallel paths, traced by Michael Sandison and Marcus Eoin respectively, overlap: one line is a steady, unwavering, and steadfast drone, while the other plays solos and varies, confident in the support of its stable counterpart."Sixtyten" is spacey and psychedelic, yet syncopated; the ghostly voices lending mystery to the final mix appear like palace spies straight out of Hieronymus Bosch's The Garden of Earthly Delights. I find funk and jazz elements in Turquoise Hexagon Sun; ambient music can be that rich, Brian Eno knows a lot about that, too, and his spirit is present on this album as well. It's about not being afraid to experiment and treating music like water: if it spills, it doesn't disappear, it simply changes shape.The bridges turn into short songs in their own right, tracks with their own distinct identity, such as "Kaini Industries" or "Bocuma", a synthesizer part that can evoke a natural waterfall, or statues coming to life at night... and "Roygbiv," which fuses a hip-hop beat with a highly symphonic, atmospheric mood, yet possesses just the right touch to feel fresh, almost New Wave, thanks to a simple keyboard, like those three-prong outlets. "Rue The Whirl" represents the brand of progressive electronica that appeals to me most; its tension builds steadily, an electronic record charged with alternating current. Through waves of sound, it achieves a passive, psychedelic atmosphere, almost a trance state, yet one not devoid of variation, as it ultimately flirts with dissonance and details like Mellotrons, striking the perfect balance between the vintage and the postmodern.The secret behind the change in sound, so percussive and featuring a sort of equidistant echo, in "Aquarius" is a slap-funk sample from the song of the same name from the movie Hair (1979). The narrative voice, the children's laughter, reminiscent of what Rickie Lee Jones used on her album Pop Pop, and those percussive variations combined to create a hybrid that was also hypnotic. Pete Standing Alone returns to those minimalist Brian Eno-esque melodies, but incorporates samples that introduce variations and shifts in rhythm, preventing the listener from settling into a routine, as the aim is to keep the sonic progression moving forward."Smokes Quantity" is rhythm with substance, a melody that provokes and leaves a lasting mark, keeping the mind wide awake; Boards of Canada offers an inward journey that challenges one's comfort zone, much like atonal music once did. Only then are we ready for "Open the Light," with its emotive, Vangelis-esque progression, for it is wrong to skip chapters that were sequenced in a specific order to prime the mood and ensure receptiveness to the climax of the penultimate track, experiencing it for what it truly is: a sonic journey.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以层叠采样、模拟合成器与节奏拼贴构建富有画面感的电子声响，短曲与长曲交替间形成含蓄的情绪起伏。作者特别肯定其对细节的掌控：持续低鸣与即兴演奏相互支撑，鼓点、刮擦声和放克切分自然嵌入氛围之中，部分桥段甚至发展成独立短歌。结尾推荐的《Rue The Whirl》以循环推进的声浪累积张力，在被动而迷幻的听感中保持结构变化，体现了独立电子音乐值得关注的实验性。

items.body: Reading back into the reviews of this recording, from over the past decades, you encounter the word “relentless” a lot, probably more than for any other album in the history of albums. It’s interesting because, when I first heard Interstellar Space , “relentless” was the word that occurred to me — right after the introductory bells of track one faded. Till then, I hadn’t realized that “relentless” was a thing that music could be, and that relentlessness was awesome. Even transcendent. It’s not a complicated record. You’ve got your tenor and drums. Each piece starts with a theme, enters the improvisation, and then winds down and restates the theme. Each improvisation travels a similar arc, beginning in a saner space, rising intensity and ecstasy, whipping us into a frenzy, then easing off into … well, not serenity, but you get close to it as you hear the shaken bells that begin the next piece. The joys of Interstellar Space come not from structural intrigue, but from the cascadingly brilliant improvs. Coltrane and Ali were both ridiculously ON that day. (Ali actually felt he had underperformed because he didn’t know they were doing a duet session until he arrived at the session.) And the duet setting makes the music almost transparent. Aside from the beauty of Trane and Ali’s playing, you also get a sense of exactly what Coltrane was trying for. His insistent explorations (relentless) are laid bare. This is an excellent entry to Coltrane’s later works. His playing is like water moving through the ground, trying to find its way through a shelf of granite. Eventually, the water finds the crevices, freezes, expands, thaws, and breaks the stone to pieces. The water always wins. A force of nature. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body:
Curating a retrospective of 40 years of recorded music is a daunting task, particularly when it is your own. Accurately representing the arc of the work and the life that created it requires frankness and acceptance. It is a process punctuated with winces and sighs and the occasional grin. Composer and improviser Jin Hi Kim experienced it all when compiling The Jin Hi Kim Collection, recently issued by Neuma. If the use of “odyssey” requires a great voyage, discovering new lands, and encountering titans, then Kim’s journey easily qualifies. Not only did she leave Korea at 23 for the US in 1980, Kim traversed an arguably greater gulf by leaving her elite training in traditional Korean music to study electronic music and composition with Lou Harrison, Terry Riley, and others. In the intervening decades, she worked with leading exponents of contemporary composition and improvisation like Kronos Quartet and Derek Bailey, and transformed the komungo, the traditional five-foot-long lute dating from the 4th Century CE, exponentially extending its sonic range through computer interfaces and signal processing.

Rediscovery accompanied the selection process for the 9-CD Collection. She was especially surprised when reviewing early works transliterating Korean music through Western instruments, or employing graphic notation. “It was created by a young mind,” Kim recently recalled with a laugh. “Sometimes it was hard to hear that’s what I did. But it was also good evidence for an archival collection. It was a wonderful feeling to look at everything I did – well, almost everything – but one thing that I was really proud about it is that there is not just one kind of music. Each piece has its Korean roots but, like I’ve said, I came to America to make new music, so I look at my 40 years of work and, yeah, I achieved that. So, it was a very satisfying process.

“When I listen to some of the improvisations, I realized how young and unafraid I was. Komungo has a limited sound compared to other instruments. When you work with virtuoso improvisers, they have vocabularies that are so rich. They are creating so many different colors and textures, but komungo has limits. It doesn’t allow you to express so much of the story. It has a meditative energy, of nothingness, of slowness. I was so brave to use this instrument with such incredible masters and to communicate with them and create music with them. I did it somehow with my inner energy. I was able to present this inner energy.”

The Collection almost equally divides Kim’s work in composition and improvisation, with five discs devoted to works for orchestra and chamber music ensembles, and four documenting improvisations with, among others, an impressive diversity of percussionists, including Gerry Hemingway, Susie Ibarra, and Tony Oxley, and string players like Bill Frisell, Min Xiao-Fen, and Hans Reichel. If anything can be read into it, the slight tilt reflects her ardent pursuit to articulate the concept of Living Tones Compositions, and how central it is to her work.

“The most important thing about the Living Tones Compositions is to convey the Korean element and philosophy through Western contemporary music,” she explained. “When I came to the United States after training in traditional Korean music, European classical music was more respected in Korea than the traditional music. They didn’t know much about American avant-garde music then, in the 1970s. I was a young musician who trained with the very best teachers and saw that I was not respected because I was not doing Western music.

“That created within me a great desire to fix that problem. You can’t fix anything, but I was young, I had a passion and a mission. I was living in the United States; I was composing for Western musicians; so how could I make this Korean idea, this Korean state of mind in making music, how could I put this together with Western music with equal respect? That was my thing. All my Living Tones Compositions come from the idea of putting together the Korean context and philosophy and Western instruments and musical context, to see how Western musicians took to the Korean attitude – not necessarily techniques, scales, anything like that – but this attitude, this state of mind. That’s what I’m doing with Living Tones music.

“Korean traditional music was once influenced by Chinese music,” Kim prefaced to explain the context and philosophy of Korean music, which she also detailed extensively in her book, Duality of Ancient Korean Roots and Western New Music. “Korean music can be divided into folk music and court music. Court music was quite different from music of ordinary people. The court was deeply influenced by ancient Chinese philosophy – yin and yang; the five elements, and ancient ancestors worship. The music wasn’t entertainment; it was ritual – that was part of both court and folk music. For ordinary people, they associated music with the shaman. For court music, there were virtuoso musicians who created an austere music, based on a philosophy of cosmic sound and abstract thinking; but for ordinary people, the shaman always took care of pain, community pain. Music was performed for celebrations of harvests and other things, but more for problems like drought, someone who is sick, some kind of problem. The shaman is always dealing with the problem of pain in their lives. They always had to sing something very sad. Her song has nothing to do with joyous things – always grief and pain. Ordinary people related to that.

“Both court and folk music had an emphasis on energy – they never thought of music as just sound. It had healing energy. In the folk community, they tried to imitate the shaman, the way she sang, shaking the notes, trying to reach out to another spirit, trying to connect heaven and earth. If you listen to a shaman’s song, there’s a very strong vibrato. The instrumentalists who don’t sing listen to this type of music; it’s very touching, very soulful, and it reflects the problems in their lives. Korean instrumentalists are all shaking, shaking their hands, shaking their instruments, shaking their notes. I play komungo, where the strings can move a lot, up and down, so you can really shake the notes and express the music in the same way as the shaman. I translate that process, that context, that spirit, into Living Tones. Each tone has its own light, and because it has its own light, its time is elastic. It is not like abstract Western time, where you count the time of each note perfectly, and you don’t have the space for microtones. There’s no time to do that in Western music. Time becomes much more open and that’s why in Korean music they don’t talk about abstract time but time in a cycle. Within that cycle, you have a lot of freedom of how to use that space with deep vibratos or any other articulation to create that intense feeling.”

The qualities Kim ascribes to Korean music are manifest in the komungo. It has a palpably plangent sound, with a bass register lower and more resonant than the guembri’s and the sting of ancient harps in its highest notes. It has a timbral luster comparable to the dark, iridescent glazes of pit-fired ceramics or the blocks of deep color that hover over the black basecoats of a Mark Rothko painting. Its dredge-like twang and the skeletal figures central to the music stop the racing, associative Western mind dead in its tracks. Even before Kim augmented the instrument with signal processing, Western improvisers had a strong attraction to the komungo. Conversely, improvisation has, over the decades, impacted Kim’s outlook.

However, Kim has a nuanced view on how improvisation has influenced her. “Influence is the result over a long period,” she elaborated, “because I played with a person one time or two times. That long period is a really deep space. It’s not that a particular musician gave me something. It is that the experience of playing with someone becomes part of my life experience. Now I look at something differently than when I was young. I understand how the universe works because of scientists and I understand how improvisation works because of improvisers. When you travel all around the world – I’ve performed in over 60 countries and have lived in some of these countries for a long time, six months or even a year – then you have an incredibly different life perspective. All of those things interest me. So, I have been influenced by many things over the decades, so that when I play with someone, it is not just that moment I am responding to; it’s everything about the other musicians: their instruments; their traditions; their culture. That gives me a very clear idea what to do.

“When I was young, I was so desperate to communicate successfully with each improviser I played with. I was trying to understand their personality; I was trying to understand their vocabulary. There have been very few times that I played on the spot without any information about the people I was playing with. I had heard them before I had the opportunity to play with them, playing with other musicians or solo. In my own way, I understood who they are. If I don’t understand them and their musical elements, I have no way to contribute anything on komungo. I have to understand their personality, their energy, how they process the music. Not all people process the same way; some people are poetic; some people are very emotional; some people are very funny. Everybody has those things happening. Understanding that was very important to me. It helped me to communicate, to hear what they were giving me, so I could give back. I listened a lot to what they were doing at a particular moment.”

Given that improvisers spanning James Newton and Elliott Sharp, and Rüdiger Carl and Oliver Lake, are heard throughout the box set, it is noteworthy that Kim singles one out to illustrate her approach to improvisation. “When I work with William Parker, he has a very deep energy in his soul,” she said of the bassist. “When I played with him, he influenced me with his deep energy. It’s really big. That influenced me to be really big. That bigness, that abundance, that tireless energy; that lets us play a really long time. He has the qualities to do something that a Korean shaman could do, playing the same idea over and over and over for a long time – trance like – but the energy becomes more powerful. William Parker has that type of energy. The bass is like the komungo; it has a deep energy and incredible power. I’m really influenced by that.”

Retrospectives like the Collection are generally considered to be merely summations, but in Kim’s case, it is more a marker of distance travelled and journeys ahead. “It reflects my continuous evolution as an artist. Throughout my musical journey, I have always searched for new ways to express myself creatively while remaining deeply rooted in my Korean musical identity.

“In essence, every work in this collection is the result of my enduring desire to elevate often-neglected Korean aesthetics, shaped alongside the freedom I found in America – a place that allowed me to pursue my artistic passions and ideas without limitation.

“Today, my perspective extends beyond national boundaries to the increasingly interconnected global community. I have aspired to use music as a spiritual and transformative force to confront social challenges. I believe this has become the new direction of my artistic journey.”

Kim’s new direction has steered her towards to uplifting marginalized subalterns and breaking through the fourth wall of the concert hall separating musicians from listeners. “Right now, because the world has changed so much, and America is now so blue, and so many people are mentally ill – I know because I recently gave a music meditation workshop at the Yale mental health center – I want to do something about community pain. I always go back to what the shaman does. I think I have sort of achieved my goal of blending Korean and Western ways of thinking with Living Tones, so right now I want to make music that the community participates in. Not necessarily well-trained musicians, but anybody who is interested. I already started on this in 2023 with a piece called ‘Ritual for Earth.’ I would like to do these things for now. I’m not anxious about my career or my next commission. I’m thinking about community pain, environmental issues like wildfires and floods, the world we are living in. So, if I have the opportunity, working with communities is what I want to do.”

items._cn_summary: 这张九碟合辑回顾了韩国作曲家兼即兴演奏家金熙四十年的创作生涯。她从韩国传统音乐出发，远赴美国师从Lou Harrison与Terry Riley学习电子音乐与作曲，将有着一千六百年历史的玄琴通过电脑接口与信号处理大幅拓展其声音范围。合辑中五张碟收录管弦乐与室内乐作品，四张碟记录她与Gerry Hemingway、Susie Ibarra、Tony Oxley等打击乐手及Bill Frisell、Min Xiao-Fen等弦乐演奏家的即兴合作。作品融合韩国传统根脉与西方实验手法，既有早期用图形记谱与西方乐器转译韩国音乐的尝试，也有后期对玄琴声音边界的持续探索。跨越传统与现代、东方与西方、作曲与即兴的多元路径，构成了这张合辑的核心价值。

items.body:
Gerry Hemingway leads a band of globe-trotters: German multi-reedist Frank Gratkowski whose recorded in the US often; pianist Izumi Kimura based in Ireland; Swiss bassist Christian Weber who’s recorded on three continents, crossing paths along the way with Yanks Oliver Lake, Ellery Eskelin, Nate Wooley, and Russ Johnson; Gerry himself, based in Lucerne since 2009.

In many ways Hemingway’s contemporary music mines his time in Anthony Braxton’s wondrous 1985-1993 quartet. The leaping staccato melody with asymmetrical phrases near the top of the 36-minute “Bau 4 Assembly” is one marker; another, the way that loose suite and the 23-minute “Slivers” use long improvised sections to tie together occasional scored episodes – not that Braxton was alone in that. And Braxton’s quartet prompted Hemingway’s duo with bandmate Marilyn Crispell, prefiguring his duo with Kimura in recent years.

On the CD, a six-minute Hemingway-Kimura improvisation is sandwiched between the long pieces, but I tend to cue up that “Third Story Variation” first, for its unbeatable interplay. The pianist and drummer catch and ride the same pulse, leaving plenty of air but also knowing how to fill various spaces along the way. Their timbral senses are fully compatible: her under-the-hood preparations tilt her sound drumward. They’ll set up a slow groove together, then she’ll use her other hand to play against it. It’s all very attentive and effective.

The longer pieces credited to Hemingway unfold like narratives, with discreet episodes, varied pacing, subgroup subplots, ways to build and dispel tension. “Slivers” is for trio, minus piano, Gratkowski leading off on squawky bass clarinet, tracked by Weber’s bass; the time feel is notably looser than the duo’s. A few minutes in, bass clarinet exits, and Frank’s re-entrance on disembodied wispy alto is placed just right: an instant orchestrator’s decision. Later there’s a section for low bass clarinet and arco bass in frictive unison under free drum rustle – suggesting Braxton’s love of the sub-basement, and the flexible trio dynamic of Gerry’s early/longtime vehicle BassDrumBone. But “Slivers” does slack off a bit between the scored tentpoles. There are times you wish the drummer would apply a firmer hand in a what-would-Billy-Higgins-do kind of way. One of Gerry’s signatures at the traps is a free-swinging–arms sense of relaxation, hitting the skins as if on the rebound, with some hits maybe dropped or delayed in transit. In the closing minutes, and on the closing theme, he can come off like someone who thinks he’s swinging harder than he is.

All four assemble for “Bau 4 Assembly” which makes up the bulk of the program. The venue Bau 4 in Altbüron, Switzerland was founded by folks in the timber business, and is located in their commercial compound. In tribute, Gerry and company play or use as beaters wood scraps retrieved from the workshop, notably heard around 10 minutes in, on a fast irregular clacky and texturally light colloquy which develops into something like pointillism with a groove (no small achievement) before flute and pedal-down piano soften things up. But not for long; in very short order, a scrapwood and piano gamelan. Midway, there’s a long-tone chapter with clarinet, and Gerry singing wavery lines into his cymbals or (says here) through metal objects, an odd effect he just about pulls off. (There’s a little Robert Wyatt in his vocal wah-wahs.) The composer and the quartet cover much ground. Elsewhere, a slow line’s melodic contours are subtly mirrored by the drums.

We won’t catalog every change-up or chapter, but near the end there’s a free-jazz blowout whose presence feels like checking a box – which is not to overlook Frank’s rapid multiphonic growls. (He’s got a great command of altissimo and pressurized reed textures.) Then they break into a loose brisk tempo, to frame that free-jazz energy. It arrives just where a non-drummer’s band would place a climactic the drum solo. Then a feint toward the Braxtonian head from half an hour earlier. A few staccato hits end things without a big fuss.

items._cn_summary: 这张现场专辑记录了杰里·海明威与一支跨国班底的即兴创作，核心气质明显承袭安东尼·布劳顿四重奏的不规则跃动、宽阔呼吸与松散叙事结构。由海明威与木村泉组成的短篇三重变奏以出色的节奏默契和音色互补见长，预制钢琴向鼓点靠拢，两人在同一律动上既留出空间又彼此填充。三重奏作品《Slivers》中，格拉特科夫斯基的低音单簧管与韦伯的贝斯形成摩擦性齐奏，木片又被用作打击素材，呼应场地木材工业背景。全员合流的《Bau 4 Assembly》以长篇展开、段落转换和群体动态构建张力，但中段推进略显松散，海明威自由挥臂的鼓风偶有失控。整体结构完整、声音层次丰富，是兼具叙事性与实验性的大编制现场记录。

items.body: The broadly ambitious Generate Music is the Prism Quartet's latest project, featuring saxophonists Timothy McAllister (soprano), Zachary Shemon (alto), Matthew Levy (tenor), and Taimur Sullivan (baritone). Formed in 1984, their mission is �To place the saxophone in unexpected contexts, expand the repertoire through new commissions, and challenge audiences.� On this eleven-track, 86-minute set, they do just that. Tyshawn Sorey | Ursula Rucker | Diane Monroe This collection includes the quartet augmented by David Gilmore (Electric guitar), David Krakauer (Klezmer clarinet), Tyshawn Sorey (Drums and percussion), Reuben Rogers (Bass), Ursula Rucker (Vocals and poetry), Susan Watts (Trumpet and vocals), and Diane Monroe (Violin). Through modern jazz arrangements, improvisations,� and spoken word, they seek to �explore the historical, cultural, and creative ties between Black and Jewish Americans.� Generate Music by PRISM Quartet, D. Gilmore, D. Krakauer, D. Monroe, R. Rogers, U. Rucker, T. Sorey, S. Watts � The opening track references �A Griot and a Cantor,� the storyteller in West African culture and the worship leader in the Jewish faith. The sonic architecture arrives with �The Unknown Common Ancestor,� which jumps between a World Saxophone Quartet-inspired sound and klezmer music with clarinet and trumpet.� � Generate Music by PRISM Quartet, D. Gilmore, D. Krakauer, D. Monroe, R. Rogers, U. Rucker, T. Sorey, S. Watts The striking and authoritative voice of Ursula Rucker narrates �Requiem for AJ.� After a dramatic overture, it sets up the narrative tension that develops across the record. Rucker tells the story of the 1964 murders of civil rights activists James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner near Philadelphia, Mississippi. On the 60th anniversary of this American tragedy, Rucker explains that they went �to register black voters (sigh)� and then she asks us to: Look up the rest of the story if you care Do you... Care? Or do you just... Do you?� With tense dramatic irony, Rucker nonchalantly states, �Poets have queries,� and the recitation ends with emphatic repetition of �Do you?�� This ten-minute powerhouse also features the band at its best with Tyshawn Sorey�s swirling drumming and David Gilmore (not to be confused with his Pink Floyd namesake) offering one of his several fiery guitar solos. It makes a fitting single, representative of the in-your-face right-left punches of improvised jazz and honest stylized performance poetry. Generate Music by PRISM Quartet, D. Gilmore, D. Krakauer, D. Monroe, R. Rogers, U. Rucker, T. Sorey, S. Watts Highlighted throughout with bursts of klezmer, often seamlessly blended with funky jazz, the Jewish tradition is especially highlighted on �Lift Every Voice and Sing.� Originally debuted in 1900, this hymn by brothers John Rosamond Johnson and James Weldon Johnson has been called a �Negro national anthem.� Here it is translated into Yiddish by Joshua Woletzshky and sung by Susan Watts, featuring violin by Diane Monroe. �Shall I continue to lie about my sadness to keep you from yours?� asks Rucker on �Let�s All Gather & Go All Together, Shall We,� offering an optimistic way forward in a world of hate. She narrates the story of a young black man in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, who is murdered by a Jewish pharmacist, exposing grief but also a way to get beyond it. Here and throughout, the music comments, prods, replies, and exuberantly jams out. Powerful, virtuosic, and close to the bone, Generate Music keeps its promise and takes another giant step in the evolution of the Prism Quartet. items._genre: avant-garde jazz / improvisation / klezmer fusion / spoken word
items._cn_summary: 这是普里姆四重奏以黑人美国人与犹太裔历史文化联结为主题的十一曲作品。萨克斯四重奏联合鼓手泰肖恩·索里、吉他手吉尔莫、克莱兹默单簧管家克拉考尔、女诗人与歌者乌尔苏拉·吕克等扩展编制，通过现代爵士即兴、克莱兹梅尔传统与 funk 节奏的交错构建声音。开场《未知的共同祖先》并置世界萨克斯四重奏式音响与克莱兹梅尔元素；《为 AJ 的安魂曲》以吕克权威而紧绷的叙述重现民权活动人士遇害事件，叠加索里旋转鼓点与吉他激烈独奏，成为全碟核心。结尾提到的《Lift Every Voice and Sing》进一步凸显犹太传统与黑人灵歌的对话。

items.album: Palagoma
items.excerpt:

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items.body: Review by meurdhek — Nearly 50 years that we've been waiting for these recordings! They have finally reached us in the form of a CD packed to the brim.Here, then, is Xalph, with its creative and warm take on Zeuhl, embracing us and happily plunging us back into the excitement of those years at the end of Magma's first incarnation, when excellent bands emerged from its orbit and carved their own paths through the lava of the world Magma had created.Besides shedding some Soleil Zeuhl light on these recordings, this edition finally sets the record straight, putting things back in order and into perspective, after the Monster M�lodies edition made two mistakes when the LP was released in 2018.The first stated: "This record contains the track 'Gya-Tei' in its entirety, a track of which only part had previously appeared on the Enneade compilation of new music, released in 1987."Yet this track had in fact already been released in its entirety on the Enneade compilation...The second claim was made with no small amount of audacity, or perhaps simply out of ignorance: "This record contains all of this legendary group's studio recordings."We now know that this was false. In fact, all the recordings on this CD had already been circulating online for decades under the title "Demos 1975-1980", albeit in inferior-sounding versions.One could even argue that the best tracks were not chosen for the Monster M�lodies LP. "Xessanderelph", "Exorde" and "Ter" keep you on the edge of your seat, and while some of the other tracks may initially seem softer, with occasional lulls, every track contains passages and endings of epic, exultant, even blazing progressive Zeuhl. This is further reinforced by the addition of vocals, which undoubtedly immerse Xalph even more deeply in the genre's established conventions, shaped by the model that bears Vander's signature, while pushing the jazz-rock aspect of their music slightly further into the background.With the exception of Gya-Tei, all the tracks presented here had therefore remained unreleased in this particular form. Nevertheless, we find the intro to "Entr�e d'Am�lie" and "Ballade � Xalph" on the LP in earlier versions that one might even prefer. The addition of soprano saxophone undoubtedly gives them a more soaring lyrical quality, while the later versions recorded at Studio Isis bring a more pronounced sense of tension, with the guitar pushed further to the forefront.In any case, if I were to indulge in a shortcut, I would say that Xessander's presents countless moments of musical grace and daring, drawn from the finest vintage of Zeuhl jazz-rock lava. It would have been a shame if we had never had the chance to enjoy them.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑收录了法国Zeuhl乐队Xalph在1975至1980年间录制的作品，历经近五十年终于以CD形式正式发行。乐评指出此前2018年黑胶版本存在错误信息，此版予以更正。音乐延续了Magma开创的Zeuhl风格，融合爵士摇滚元素，加入人声与高音萨克斯，强化了该流派的仪式感与史诗性张力。吉他被推向更突出的位置，录音在Studio Isis完成，呈现出比早期LP版本更具紧绷感的质感。评论特别推荐《Xessanderelph》《Exorde》《Ter》等曲目，认为这些作品展现了Zeuhl熔岩般的爆发力与大胆构思，虽部分段落初期听感偏柔，但每首都包含史诗般的高潮结尾，兼具爵士摇滚的复杂律动与前卫摇滚的结构野心。

items.body: Review by Logan — The history of Boc Maxima functions like a rogue transmission. Distributed as a private 1996 cassette to a small inner circle of family and friends, it eventually leaked into the early-2000s file-sharing ether and became a foundational internet myth. Rather than a mere collection of loose bedroom demos, the tape serves as the unredacted genetic blueprint for what Boards of Canada would become. Context alters the architecture. A sound wave does not change its geometry, but its impact shifts based on the reified bounds of the sequence. Sequenced between dark, lo-fi vignettes and deliberate, haunting fade-ins, these familiar melodies lose their polished studio insulation. The timeline functions less like a passive playlist and more like a continuous midnight broadcast.The movement of this tape carries the uncanny dimensions of The Twilight Zone, where science meets superstition, alongside the OBLIVION signal in Cronenberg's Videodrome, and the unrepeatable frequency of the 1977 Wow! signal. The bleeding transitions carry a distinct Blue Jam late-night radio logic. The sequencing introduces an invasive quality that alters how the listening space decodes this familiar pastoral nostalgia, inducing a state of quiet suspension where childhood memory and cold, apocalyptic dread exist in an uneasy harmony. Long live the new flesh.
items._cn_summary: 《Boc Maxima》是Boards of Canada于1996年以私人卡带形式在亲友小圈子中流传的早期作品，后经文件交换网络扩散，成为互联网早期音乐神话之一。这张专辑并非松散的卧室demo集合，而是乐队日后成熟风格的原始基因图谱。乐评聚焦于磁带独特的序列编排逻辑：低保真片段与刻意安排的淡入交替排列，消解了旋律在录音室中的打磨感，营造出连续午夜广播般的连续性。阴暗的音色质感中渗出田园式怀旧，与末世焦虑形成不安的共存。乐评将其与《阴阳魔界》的诡异维度、克罗南伯格《录影带谋杀案》中的OBLIVION信号以及1977年Wow!信号等文化意象并置，指出这张作品通过侵入性的聆听空间重构，构建了一种童年记忆与冷峻恐惧并存的状态。评论以"新肉身万岁"作结，强化了其作为邪典文本的定位。

items.body: Front Line Assembly’s “Epitaph” turns 25 this year. Metropolis Records released the electro-industrial and EBM album on 8 October 2001, the eleventh full-length studio album by the Vancouver band led by Bill Leeb and Chris Peterson. The record marked Front Line Assembly‘s return to Metropolis Records after the band left the label in October 1999. “Epitaph” runs ten tracks and 54:57, recorded at Cryogenic Studio and produced by Leeb and Peterson. Greg Reely handled mixing and engineering, Brian Gardner mastered the album, and Dave McKean supplied the artwork and design. The tracklist runs “Haloed”, “Dead Planet”, “Backlash”, “Epitaph”, “Everything Must Perish”, “Conscience”, “Decoy”, “Insolence”, “Krank It Up” and “Existance”, the last of which folds in the hidden track “Submerged” after a minute of silence. Metropolis also issued a digipak edition limited to 25,000 copies carrying that bonus track. “Everything Must Perish”, released 11 September 2001, was the only single taken from the album. Bill Leeb told Side-Line at the time that “Epitaph” broke with the band’s earlier reliance on film dialogue samples: “This is the first time we quit using movie samples.” He added: “Sampling is an artform which was criticised in the beginning, but now it’s a respected artform with big money in it. It’s a big business where I don’t feel at ease any longer.” Artoffact Records re-released ‘Epitaph’ on limited edition vinyl in 2015. About Front Line Assembly Bill Leeb founded Front Line Assembly in Vancouver, British Columbia, in 1986 after leaving Skinny Puppy, where he had performed under the stage name Wilhelm Schroeder. Rhys Fulber worked with Leeb from the same period as an early, unofficial collaborator, and Michael Balch became an official member on keyboards and programming in 1988. The band’s debut album, “The Initial Command”, came out on the Belgian label KK at the end of 1987, followed by “State of Mind” on the German label Dossier in January 1988 and “Corrosion” the same year, licensed to Wax Trax! for North America. Balch left after the Gashed Senses & Crossfire tour in 1989 to join Ministry and Revolting Cocks, and Fulber stepped in as an official member. “Gashed Senses & Crossfire” (1989) gave the band its first chart entry, with “Digital Tension Dementia” reaching No. 45 on Billboard’s Hot Dance Club Songs. “Caustic Grip” followed in 1990, the album that began Front Line Assembly’s long-running partnership with mixer and engineer Greg Reely and introduced more guitar-driven material. Chris Peterson debuted as a live percussionist on the accompanying tour before later becoming a full-time member. “Tactical Neural Implant” (1992) brought a more melodic, sample-heavy direction, and “Millennium” (1994) became the band’s first industrial metal record, featuring session guitar from Devin Townsend, who also played on “Hard Wired” (1995). Fulber left in 1997 to concentrate on producing Fear Factory, and Peterson took over his role as the band moved toward the electronica and big-beat leanings of “[FLA]vour of the Weak” (1997) and “Implode” (1999). In October 1999 the band left Metropolis Records; “Epitaph”, produced by Leeb and Peterson and issued on 8 October 2001, marked its return to that label. Peterson departed after finishing work on the album, and Fulber rejoined in 2003 for “Civilization” (2004). Beyond the main discography, Leeb has led the side project Delerium since 1987, and members have worked on Noise Unit, Conjure One (Fulber), Cyberaktif (Leeb with Skinny Puppy’s cEvin Key and Dwayne Goettel) and other spin-offs. Front Line Assembly went on to release “Artificial Soldier” (2006), “Improvised Electronic Device” (2010), “Echogenetic” (2013), “Wake Up the Coma” (2019) and “Mechanical Soul” (2021), the last featuring guest appearances from Jean-Luc De Meyer of Front 242 and Dino Cazares of Fear Factory. The band caught up with Side-Line on the state of the group in 2024, with Leeb and Fulber both still in the current lineup. “Epitaph” remains the band’s eleventh studio album and, twenty-five years on, the record that reopened its relationship with Metropolis Records.
items._cn_summary: Front Line Assembly 2001年发行的第十一张全长专辑，由Bill Leeb与Chris Peterson共同制作，延续其冷峻、压迫性的工业电子路线，同时保留更直接的吉他驱动力。专辑共十首曲目，标准版时长54分57秒，结尾曲后藏有《Submerged》。本辑首次放弃电影对白采样，反映乐队对既有创作方法的主动调整。文中主要提供发行版本、曲目名单、制作人员及乐队早期历史，缺少对具体声响与旋律的深入评论，但整体资料完整，仍能体现其电子工业体系下的持续发展与场景影响力。

items.body: Label: ECM Records, 2026 Personnel - Enrico Rava: trumpet; Joe Lovano: tenor saxophone, tarogato; Matteo Paggi: trombone; Francesco Diodati: guitar; Francesco Ponticelli: bass; Evita Pollidoro: drums, vocals. Illustrious Italian trumpeter and composer Enrico Rava, a longtime force on the European jazz scene, returns with his Fearless Five ensemble, welcoming guest saxophonist Joe Lovano, a powerhouse improviser who had collaborated with the bandleader on the live recording Roma (ECM, 2019). All members of the quintet contribute compositions, trusting the bandleader's candidly investigative approach that opposes rigid perceptions. Rava's " Certi Angoli Segreti ", an exceptionally beautiful tune first recorded in 1998, gracefully materializes with beautiful color shades. Francesco Diodati's guitar gives it a particular touch, later soloing with motivic ability and acerbic distortion; Francesco Ponticelli's dynamic bass builds a solid foundation with drummer Evita Polidoro; Lovano's storytelling comes with delightful details; trombonist Matteo Paggi's expressions are grounded and exploratory; and Rava excels in his improvisational fluctuations—sometimes angular and outside, other times hypnotically flowing and distinctively melodic. Rava brings two other previously recorded pieces: " Hitchcock at the Beach ", whose balladic feeling and original beauty are preserved despite emerging here most as a collaborative voice-trumpet meditation; and the exciting " Bowery Dance ", which evokes Rava's New York years with an electrified intro, authoritative bass double-stops, and a crisp backbeat. Lovano and Rava improvise with fire, rejoicing in unison lines in support of their declarations. Lovano is credited with a couple of distinct compositions. The open-ended " Sun Rava " is full of possibilities, incorporating sharp staccato blows, buoyant swing impulses, and clever pedal points, also featuring improvised dialogues between Rava and Paggi, and then Diodati and Lovano, before the saxophonist rambles freely over the bass-and-drums bedrock. " Tone, Shape, and Colours ", a free improvisation based on a riff by Lovano, brings the horn players together in lively conversation. If the rhythm section kicks into high gear on Lovano's pieces, it eases into the softer lyrical flow of Diodati's " Sin Peso ", a burnished ballad suggesting a bolero feel, and Polidoro's " Le Mie Gambe ", which, unfolding in 3/4, features the drummer as a vocalist of surprising intensity. Since the early '70s, Rava—who turned 87 in August—has led a series of highly rewarding albums, and Corners is no exception. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Certi Angoli Segreti ► 06 - Tune, Shape, and Colours ► 08 - Bowery Dance

items._cn_summary: 意大利小号手Enrico Rava领衔的Fearless Five六重奏，与美国萨克斯大师Joe Lovano合作，在ECM厂牌下呈现了一张融合创作型爵士与自由即兴的专辑。每位成员贡献原创作品，Rava的三首曲目——包括首次录制于1998年的抒情曲《Certi Angoli Segreti》、改编自早期版本的《Hitchcock at the Beach》和充满纽约回忆的《Bowery Dance》——展示了其从旋律流动到棱角即兴的多面风格。Lovano贡献了开放式的《Sun Rava》与基于即兴riff的《Tune, Shape, and Colours》，鼓手Polidoro以出人意料的声乐表现参与其中。乐评特别强调了小号与萨克斯的对话质感、吉他手Diodati的尖锐失真独奏以及节奏组的动态支撑，整张专辑在抒情叙事与自由探索之间取得了平衡。

items.body: Rather than resolving its strange machinery, Noxi Melank leaves it in motion—a collection of damaged systems, unstable rhythms, and modular forms continually finding new ways to become something else. Blurry to the senses, roughened around the edges Noxi Melank by ignatius   One of our favorite crafters of modular abstraction, glitch, and electronic noise, Ignatius (Buried In Time) makes a striking debut with Noxi Melank for Evel. Across eight pieces, sound worlds are explored, eroded, fragmented, and reshaped from start to finish. A surreal, broken rhythmic transition opens the nearly 10-minute opus “IdleDeep,” where blips, bleeps, echoes, scattered voices, and subdued electronic residue flicker beneath a slippery surface of decay. “GenderLimo” picks up the pace, remaining subtle, melankolic, and abstract as drifting, crumpled tones and drones take shape. Its sounds feel almost timeless, like abandoned and dented machines searching for somewhere to restart, mutate, and build unfamiliar worlds. As Ignatius’ glitch language unfolds piece by piece, each movement is marked by an unusually astute clarity within the noise. “Editorial,” for instance, reveals itself through Autechre meets Syl Kougaï-infused rhythmic deformation and energy, where modular structures seem to buckle, reconfigure, and find new momentum. While low-end rattling soundscapes provide a constant benchmark for Noxi Melank, Ignatius finds particular comfort in unusual time signatures—blurry to the senses, roughened around the edges, yet always moving forward with the precision of a practiced sound sculptor. Translucent structures of decay and erosion :: As the album persists, its tracks remain connected through an elusive, surreal logic. “Nonsequitirs” and “Locations” are especially revealing, unfolding as downtempo, almost translucent electroacoustic structures of decay and erosion. Dark passages maneuver through electronic debris, allowing fragments of rhythm and texture to surface before disappearing again. Closing with “SloxiEnds,” Ignatius shifts toward a more upbeat final chapter. Its Tri Repetae-like abstraction carries an unexpected sense of beauty, gradually transforming through layers of modular distortion—something the cover art depicts with uncanny precision—before arriving at an almost Eastern-sounding flourish. Rather than resolving its strange machinery, Noxi Melank leaves it in motion—a collection of damaged systems, unstable rhythms, and modular forms continually finding new ways to become something else. Noxi Melank is available on Evel. [Bandcamp] Noxi Melank by ignatiusThe post Ignatius :: Noxi Melank (Evel) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由模块化合成器驱动，呈现为一套受损运转的声学系统。八首曲目贯穿碎片化节奏、不稳定拍号与电子残响，构建出模糊、腐蚀、不断自我重组的声音景观。作品在噪点中保持异常清晰的层次感，节奏结构如机械般弯折、重新配置并获得新动力；低频的隆隆声作为贯穿基准，异常拍号与透明感的电声结构交替出现。专辑以近乎东方的收尾作为终章，整体拒绝收束，机器始终处于运转中，持续变异并构筑陌生的世界。它适合熟悉电子实验与解构主义聆听脉络的听众，厂牌Evel属于小众独立发行。

items.body: Mathias Villard is a very promising sound artist and Past Radiance can easily figure among my top favorite albums for this year. Exquisite, wistful, cinematic, alluring and emotionally transportive. For fans of Alessandro Cortini, Bvdub, Loscil, Markus Fjellström and Terence Hannum. Once more, Affin proves to be in the first league concerning modern-day ambient-lush drone music. The album flows like a gigantic oceanic movement Past Radiance by Mathias Villard   Mathias Villard is a French sound artist now based in Düsseldorf, Germany. He is a new face in the world of ambient-drone and orchestral cinematic electronica, but his debut album finds the best possible way to bring it to a larger international audience, thanks to a contract with key indie label Affin (headed by Joachim Spieth). Affin already presents an immense catalog of advanced electronic music with a strong interest in densely layered soundscapes, emotional cinematic escapism and ambient-techno waves. Numerous well-established projects and names are part of the catalogue, among others Pepo Galán and Markus Guentner (with his magnificent Black Dahlia reviewed on Igloo). Past Radiance appears to be a high-class textured ambient release with a strong melodious-moody component that will leave you speechless. If you are fond of lush sonic textures and enveloping electronic sequences sustained by grainy repetitive melodies surrounded by a vast, spacious aura, there is no doubt that this album will reach your heart. The gently sinuous parts and soothing ambiences are powerfully seconded by deep and slowly bassy lines which definitely add more depth and strength to the pieces. Difficult to pick out one piece in particular, as the album flows like a gigantic oceanic movement with rare sonic engulfment. Some lighter moments appear from time to time :: In a track such as “Debris,” this mysterious sonic approach and spacious treatment reach full development: a really massive, cascading and compelling piece. This album integrates a sumptuous sense of motion which meets quite devastating, heart-stirring, almost gloomy but always pleasant melodies. Some lighter moments appear from time to time, as in the curiously pulsating, chilling and bassy “Haze.” The success of this album lies in the meticulously crafted compositional mode but also in the solid technical production. All in all, Mathias Villard is a very promising sound artist and his album can easily figure among my top favorite albums for this year. Exquisite, wistful, cinematic, alluring and emotionally transportive. For fans of Alessandro Cortini, Bvdub, Loscil, Markus Fjellström and Terence Hannum. Once more, this label proves to be in the first league concerning modern-day ambient-lush drone music. Past Radiance is available on Affin. [Bandcamp] The post Mathias Villard :: Past Radiance (Affin) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.
items._cn_summary: Mathias Villard 的首张专辑呈现了高密度的氛围-嗡鸣质感，音乐如同一场宏大的海洋运动缓缓铺展。层层叠加的织体与颗粒状重复旋律构成了核心音色语言，深沉的低音线条在轻盈处与昏暗处之间游走，形成开阔的空间感与缓慢的吞噬感。作品在精致的作曲结构与扎实的制作技术之间取得平衡，旋律带有忧郁却不失温和的质地，既有电影化的远景也有亲密的近景。部分曲目中可感知到脉动的节奏暗示和低频的驱动，但整体仍以静态的环境氛围为主导。该作品适合在沉浸式聆听场景中展开，文本层面的描述虽丰富但音乐本体仍需由听者自行在长时段中验证其情感张力的深度。

items.body: Review by Logan — Returning to Hi Scores after spending time with the heavy, dark sound of Inferno is like finding an old, clean blueprint before it weathered. This 1996 EP finds the Sandison brothers at a time when their geometric tracking methods were sharp and exposed, before their focus shifted toward deep analogue erosion. It occupies a distinct place in their discography, bypassing the fragile sentimentality of their later records. The sound functions as a raw, intense environment rather than electronic escapism, following an internal logic that aligns with how my own mind navigates structure.The title track, "Hi Scores", relies on a clinical drive. Spending time with their wider catalogue highlights the unconventional nature of this upfront electro-funk grid. Originally released on Manchester's experimental Skam label, it establishes a stark, unpolished baseline belonging to the sharp mathematical grids of the mid-nineties IDM scene rather than a childhood memory. It reveals a naked skeletal frame, showing basic programming choices before the arrangements were buried in rich, atmospheric grime."Turquoise Hexagon Sun" is positioned next. Observing how this piece functions later on Music Has the Right to Children makes its placement here notable. It introduces the loop-based geometry and hexagonal motifs they would reference for decades. Yet, for all its melodic layers, it holds an unsettling tension. It is a track I turn off when the kids are around, since the underlying textures feel less like a comforting memory and more like a displaced, menacing transmission.The transition into "Nlogax" requires a distinct mental shift. Instead of a soft fade, the drop is sharp and jarring. The track triggers a physical response. The microtonal dissonance and aggressive, detuned synth hook warp the stereo field, producing a genuine sensation of vertigo and physical nausea."June 9th" follows this pitch instability, bringing a state of sensory hyper-vigilance. By layering skittering, fast percussion elements over a lagging breakbeat and burying muffled melodies under a low-end thrum, the duo compresses the perception of space, creating a claustrophobic acoustic environment. The complex, cinematic logic shares an architectural layout with The Future Sound of London's 1994 release, Lifeforms. Both share an uncompromising, alien framework that rejects simple dancefloor trends. On a surface listen, Hi Scores can seem disjointed, but immersion in this middle section shows how the segments serve a rigid purpose.The intensity of these tracks relates directly to the literal mechanical wow and flutter effect running through the tape machines. The severe pitch warps build an environment that feels suffocating, forcing a physical confrontation across the enteric nervous system."Seeya Later" works on an interesting psychological plane. Having tracked its connection back to Twoism, the track utilises heavy, drifting synth pads to tie the upfront grooves to the end of the record, drawing the brain down into a heavy twilight trance.The final track, "Everything You Do Is a Balloon", serves as a clear blueprint for their subsequent discography. In this non-sentimental context, however, the track offers little safe haven or comforting relief. It feels off-kilter, trading easy nostalgia for a heavy, visceral sonic power. Starting with a fragile, melancholic synth melody before dropping into a slow-motion hip-hop breakbeat, it functions less as a comforting exit and more as a substantial climax that carries the electro-acoustic DNA that would later anchor the dense harmonic textures of The Campfire Headphase.Over time, Hi Scores has realised its full potential as a five-star record for me. It operates more like a raw template for psychological disruption than a standard piece of auditory expression. Spending time with all of their albums reinforces the essential nature of this blueprint, landing as an intense, disorienting, and highly effective release.
items._cn_summary: 这张1996年EP展现了Boards of Canada早期未被氛围侵蚀的原始状态，呈现出与后来作品截然不同的冷峻面貌。评论深入剖析了各曲目的结构逻辑：标题曲以机械化驱动的电气化网格构建骨架，缺乏后期作品中常见的怀旧滤镜；'Turquoise Hexagon Sun'引入循环几何与六角形动机，旋律层下暗藏不安张力；'Nlogax'则以微分音不协和与失谐合成器钩子制造眩晕与生理不适。评论将这些声音策略与磁带机物理失真、FSOL的'Lifeforms'等参照并置，指出专辑中段如何通过密集的跳切打击乐与压缩空间感形成压迫性声场。整体乐评聚焦于创作方法论的解剖，强调这张作品作为裸露蓝图而非完整建筑的存在价值，适合对IDM场景与技术美学感兴趣的听众。

items.body: One of several promising artists emerging from a wave of new blood in the DMV-area scene, Will Graham’s adventurous solo project Vasterian is still in the process of defining his sound. His first tape Static Dreams employed heavy use of radio to conjure a sputtering soundscape full of dead air and hiss, a stark contrast to the inaugural live set I saw him play earlier this year that consisted of bracing, bellowing power electronics. Though his output thus far doesn’t display a consistent style (far from a bad thing, to be sure), there’s certainly a consistent level of intent and execution. Brand new C44 Turn Around plays like an attempt to flesh out the middle ground between the disparate extremes of the debut release and performance, and a successful attempt at that. Graham structures the two sides around texture shifts between the garbled warbles of intercepted transmissions and the screech of analog feedback, opting for a patient freeform progression with plenty of room to breathe. The A-spanning “On Plummer’s Island” [sic] blooms slowly and steadily, with wounded, barely legible speech giving way to oscillating static rent with high-frequency slice ‘n dice. When the track hits its peak it’s thrilling, so howling and unstable that it feels like the tape is going to burn right through your deck. The facing pair of the title cut and “Tracing the Spiral / Smooth Character” are more pensive. Both feel fragile and vulnerable in their raw simplicity, especially when Graham flips on the vocal mic at the end of the latter and lays down some agonized shouts over a seething mass of minor harmony, a more elegiac take on the cathartic aggression found in his work as Comfort & Critique. It’s a strong and haunting conclusion that offers a late anchor to the preceding potpourri and pays off the snatches of vocals heard throughout. Turn Around may have worked better as, say, a C30 (“On Plummer’s Island” especially starts to drag toward the end) and gets a bit bogged down by its own eclecticism, the abundance of creativity and passion make it memorable—and replayable. Copies are available from the label via email: landscapesuicideproductions@gmail.com.

items._cn_summary: Vasterian 是 DMV 地区涌现的实验音乐人 Will Graham 的个人项目。C44 卡带《Turn Around》试图在其首作《Static Dreams》的电台噪音拼贴与现场呈现的粗粝暴力电子之间寻找中间地带。整张专辑围绕两极质感展开：A 面以截获式无线电传输的失真呜鸣与模拟反馈的尖啸交替铺陈，自由即兴式缓慢推进，留出大量呼吸空间；B 面则更为沉思脆弱，终曲中人声嘶吼与暗流涌动的小调和声形成挽歌式的爆发，与他另一个项目 Comfort & Critique 中的宣泄性攻击相呼应。评论认为作品虽因兼容并蓄略显拖沓，但创意密度与情感强度使其具备反复回听的价值。
