items.body: “Some endings don’t wait They arrive before you do” There is a peculiar humiliation in realizing that a relationship has ended while you were still making plans for it. Familiar routines can keep the illusion going for weeks: another message, another evening together, another promise you have learned to accept without examining too closely. Then some ordinary detail makes the situation impossible to explain away, and you find yourself catching up with a loss that has already happened. It’s the emotional equivalent of arriving late to a funeral party: the bar is empty, and the deviled eggs are already gone, and yet you’re still expecting the deceased to call you back. That liminal stretch between an ending and the moment you finally recognize it is the pulse of “No Flowers in June,” the latest single from Italian darkwave duo Soft Scent. A frantic bassline drives relentlessly onward as the synths press in around it, giving the track the jittery resolve of someone who’s just realized that standing still may be the worst thing to do. Moving on takes effort—especially when some part of you is still waiting for the other person to show up. Anna “MissLucifer” and Sara “Felina Noir” formed Soft Scent in 2023 in Italy’s Marche region, and the track is the first single from their forthcoming second album, Mother’s Ruin. Its restless movement draws on coldwave, old EBM, post-punk, the clipped propulsion of punk, and a glossy electronic abrasion that keeps the familiar ingredients feeling unsettled. At odd moments, the song seems to sit somewhere between Björk and Sigue Sigue Sputnik, which sounds ridiculous until you hear the vocal drama and synthetic sleaze brushing past one another. The song is about an ending, although not one of those glamorous endings rock music usually prefers. Nobody is smashing a mirror or walking dramatically into traffic. This is the more common variety: the thing is already over, and you are late to your own realization. Soft Scent refuses to overplay the tragedy. The arrangement holds its dark-disco poise: the bass stays restless, the electronics keep the pressure on. The hurt is unmistakable, but the song never crumples theatrically to make its point. That restraint cuts deeper than a dozen grand breakdowns ever could. The song’s video sets the band on a shadow-drenched stage, purple light pooling around them as candles and flowers frame the scene. It might have slipped into goth by numbers, but something stranger stirs—especially beside the album’s dried and ceramic blooms, and its Victorian Lover’s Eye imagery. Romance has survived, it seems, though never unwatched. Watch the video for No Flowers in June below: The title of Soft Scent’s forthcoming second studio album, Mother’s Ruin, comes from the old Victorian name for gin, which gives the album its larger framework: comfort and damage sharing the same glass. “No Flowers in June” fits neatly into that idea because it concerns the moment after escape has stopped working. You get your temporary relief, your little private holiday from consequence, and eventually consequence finds the forwarding address. No Flowers In June was recorded with Gianluca Lo Presti and mixed and mastered by William Faith, and thankfully nobody has polished it into sterility. It still has elbows. It still has that slightly unfriendly quality good dark music ought to possess. Soft Scent are not reinventing darkwave here, and that is probably beside the point. They are doing something more difficult. They are making it sound like it still has somewhere to go. Mother’s Ruin is expected in late 2026. In the meantime, order No Flowers in June here. items.body:
The brotherhood of foundational European avant garde bassists gets smaller with each passing year. And among those still living, some are either inactive for various reasons or working in other fields, musical or otherwise. So, the subset of ones still going is a small but precious list.

Among them is the Netherlands’ Arjen Gorter. Ask even a relatively informed listener of European avant garde jazz about him and almost invariably the first association will be Willem Breuker, and more specifically his Kollektief. Gorter did anchor that group for the entirety of its existence (1975-2010, with a retrospective farewell tour coming after Breuker’s death) alongside drummer Rob Verdurmen, allowing Breuker and a rotating cast of string and horn players (though trombonist Bernard Hunnekink was another stalwart) to navigate complex and subversive music, confident that a strong foundation would always support them. But like Jimmy Cobb always being referenced first and sometimes only as the last living participant of Kind of Blue after Miles Davis died in 1991, Gorter’s career, still ongoing, is hardly exclusive to his work with Breuker.

Gorter was born in Amsterdam on January 2nd, 1948 and he has resided in the Dutch capital his whole life. His road to the bass was a circuitous one. As he wrote in an email, “I liked the accordion when I was very young. It was common in the Amsterdam streets of the ‘50s, but the tunes that my teacher made me play were too silly, so that did not last. My dad imported musical instruments. He brought a slightly damaged ukulele home and so at around 11 I tried playing along with the nightly jazz broadcasts on French and Belgian radio. The father of a friend had a small jazz collection and I loved the Art Blakey Blue Note 45s, the Monk LP and the other stuff he had. So that ukulele was replaced by a guitar. I started jamming in our attic with friends and others and at some point someone brought a double bass upstairs and left it there for six months. I had fun playing it and managed to buy it from him once he showed up again.”

During high school Gorter played guitar in a band for school dances, repertoire ranging from period rock tunes to jazz compositions. He began college in 1966, aiming to study political science and sociology, the same year he first worked professionally with Breuker, having heard the older reed player’s bands around town and once playing with him at a jam session. Gorter was invited to join a new Breuker group, which performed at the Loosdrecht Jazz Competition as a sextet, then expanded to almost two-dozen musicians for the final stage. This group would make Litany for the 14th of June 1966 (Relax) in late October 1966, Gorter’s recording debut alongside two other bassists, the much older Dick van der Capellen and Victor Kaihatu.

Gorter would balance university and performing for a few years. During this time, he would work with Germany’s Gunter Hampel, appearing on his April 1968 Wergo date Gunter Hampel Group + Jeanne Lee and participating in the November 1968 Total Music Meeting in Berlin, where photo evidence has him in a bizarre encounter with Hampel, John McLaughlin, Sonny Sharrock, Pharoah Sanders, Roy Ayers, Laurie Allan, and Roel Kroes. 1969 saw even more activity: more Hampel work, including the album The 8th of July 1969 (inaugurating his Birth imprint); playing on German trumpeter Manfred Schoof’s FMP release European Echoes and being part of the Peter Brötzmann Oktett at the International Holy Hill Jazz Meeting (alongside Buschi Niebergall and Peter Kowald; Richard Williams’ review of European Echoes in the March 14th, 1970 issue of Melody Maker saying, “It’s an astonishingly powerful performance, with particularly superb work by Dudek, Bailey and the three basses, who play a really fantastic trio section.”). Gorter is also heard on the Live at The Bohemia Jazzclub recording by Hans Dulfer’s Soulbrass Inc., as well as a track with Breuker and Han and Peter Bennink heard on the Instant Composers Pool cheese box. As Gorter recalled, “I managed to juggle both activities until the end of 1969, but I was more on the road than in Amsterdam and had to make a choice and I chose the activity that gave me way more satisfaction.”

During the first half of the ‘70s, Gorter and Breuker did not work together often, at least as can be gleaned from available recordings: Hampel’s People Symphony (Birth, 1970) and part of his group that participated in German avant garde composer Hans Werner Henze’s Der Langwierige Weg In Die Wohnung Der Natascha Ungeheuer; and an unofficial Amsterdam recording from 1973 under Breuker’s leadership and a live date from Leo Cuypers in 1974, both with groups prefiguring the Kollektief (Cuypers was its first pianist). Otherwise Gorter was busy – again, at least on record – with Hans Dulfer, Kees Hazevoet, Theo Loevendie, Alexander Von Schlippenbach, and the Irène Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl Quartet. The latter two were significant. Gorter was part of the second iteration of Schlippenbach’s Globe Unity Orchestra, Niebergall and Kowald in tow once more (a 1970 Berlin Jazz Festival performance released in 2001) and the Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl group that was active for several years. “I met Rudiger in Wuppertal, that was a new jazz center by itself thanks to Peter Brötzmann and Peter Kowald,” wrote Gorter. “Sometimes I stayed at the studio that he shared with guitar wizard Hans Reichel. When Irene and Rudiger started playing together, they asked me to join and we played many places in the early ‘70s, with Heinrich Hock, Louis Moholo, or Alan Bateman on drums.” That band made only one full album, 1974’s Goose Pannée (FMP) but did have a track on the For Example - Workshop Freie Musik 1969 - 1978, the FMP boxed set.

1974-75 was an important period for two other reasons. Besides the aforementioned collaborations as well as work with the Boy Edgar Big Band and the small groups of Maurice Horsthuis and Toon van Vliet, Gorter was one of the musicians who helped establish Amsterdam’s Bimhuis, ultimately one of Europe’s premier venues for avant garde music, performing on its October 1st, 1974 opening night with the Burton Greene Quartet. Then in March 1975, Breuker asked Gorter to be a member of his Kollektief. Gorter described the group’s music as such: “Willem’s music had a lot of freedom. There were often tightly arranged written sections that would suddenly end and then the fun was to play on as if the arrangement continued – there was usually no such thing as chord changes – or to let the thing fall off a cliff ... Anyway, the music always felt fresh to play, even after many concerts, and there was a great mix of individual input and group discipline and cooperation. The Kollektief’s music linked the recognizable to the unexpected, often in 90-degree turns. It was surprising but accessible. For us musicians there was a wide spectrum of activities, from theater plays to movie music to interpretations of classical music and a lot of traveling to places where we found appreciative audiences, ranging from Australian school children to Chinese businessmen.”

The Kollektief would go on to make over three dozen albums, mostly released on Breuker’s BV Haast label, and perform all over the world, including during the Klap op de Vuurpijl (roughly, Top It All Off) Festival, taking place over five days at the end of each year from 1976-2005. Its book mixed Breuker and other band member pieces with tunes from various pages of the Great American Songbook and drawn from the classical canon, as well as other sources, presented in a highly theatrical manner best appreciated live and mixing in humor in refreshing contrast to the dour stage demeanor of many an improviser.

As busy as the Kollektief would keep him, Gorter still pursued other projects, some including fellow Kollektief members, including Breuker, and only existing on stages, such as groups under the leadership of Maarten van Norden, Sean Bergin, Boy Raaymakers, Pierre Courbois, Nedly Elstak, Jasper van ‘t Hof, Misha Mengelberg, and others. A representative sampling of those can be found in the archive of the Bimhuis (https://www.bimhuis.nl/archief); when he was in Amsterdam, this would be Gorter’s home near his home.

But there were also ones documented as albums: Maine, the 1975 collaboration of American trombonist Roswell Rudd with Dulfer, Gorter, and drummer Martin van Duynhoven, was made up of music by Sonny Rollins and Rudd (who had been coming to and working in the Netherlands since the mid ‘60s both with the New York Art Quartet and also locals like Loevendie). There were two 1977 dates by Cuypers, Zeeland Suite also including another bassist in South African expatriate Harry Miller; the 1979 Maarten Van Norden/Boy Raaymakers quartet date Chicken Song, completed by drummer Peter Nykyruj (of Mike Osborne fame); and a pair of 1980 albums spearheaded by the aforementioned trumpeter/composer Elstak (and released on his Coreco label; Gorter had loosely studied harmony with him in the ‘60s): To Build was led by Soesja Citroen’s name, who was one of five singers alongside Elstak, Breuker, Gorter, and Van Duynhoven for Sad Trumpets. The most significant, at least in terms of international exposure, came in July 1984, when Gorter, Mengelberg, and Bennink joined forces with two Americans, soprano saxophonist Steve Lacy and trombonist George Lewis, for the Soul Note release Change of Season (Music Of Herbie Nichols). Another important recording came 13 years later with Legendary: The 27th of May 1997, in a reunion with Hampel, who was fêting his seminal Heartplants SABA album from 1965 with original participants Courbois, Schlippenbach, and Schoof, Gorter standing in for his late friend Buschi Niebergall. One interesting takeaway from this is that it is often thought that after Breuker split with his fellow Instant Composers Pool founders Mengelberg and Bennink there were two distinct worlds in Dutch avant garde jazz; however, there were musicians like Gorter who operated in both spheres.

The new millennium found Gorter in several new projects: the mostly American blues/jazz band New Texas Swing from American saxophonist and then fellow Kollektief member Alex Coke with singer Tina Marsh and drummer John Betsch; the aptly named though horn-heavy Drummers Double Bill from Arend Niks and Verdurmen; 2000 recording The Compositions Of Eric Dolphy (BV Haast) with Coke, Breuker, Eric Vloeimans, Frank van Bommel, and John Engels; and Bo Van De Graaf’s I Compani; and the Rahsaan Roland Kirk “tribute” band Reeds & Deeds, also put together by Van De Graaf.

The Dolphy project had a personal resonance for Gorter, more specifically a much younger version of himself. In 1964, when he was 16, Gorter attended the Charles Mingus Sextet performance at Amsterdam’s Concertgebouw, a band with Dolphy, Johnny Coles, Clifford Jordan, Jaki Byard, and Dannie Richmond, which Gorter calls “the best ever ... Halfway through a trumpet solo by Johnny Coles, Eric left the stage while playing and walked into the hall. He ended up right next to my seat, way in the back. For a 16-year-old, that may have been a life-changing experience.” In 2011, Gorter was given the opportunity to celebrate Dolphy once more with a concert at the Bimhuis: “Eric Dolphy at The Five Spot Revisited,” with the legendary recording’s repertoire played by himself, Tom Arthurs, Rudi Mahall/Alex Coke (as his bass clarinet and saxophone/flute sides), Benoît Delbecq, and John Betsch.

Gorter joined the multimedia ensemble I Compani, founded by Van De Graaf in 1985, in 2010. As he wrote, “Bo van de Graaf just called it quits for I Compani, which I understand but regret. He led that band for 40 years through great adventures and I was happy to participate since 2010 or so. If anyone is comparable to Breuker in the amount of initiatives he took, it is him. Original pieces are blended with film music and live video, in various lineups from septet to 18-piece band. His music has the space, freedom and versatility of Breuker’s, but in a different way. Fun!”

When asked about the European scene in which he came up, Gorter replied, “At that time every European city had a very original and recognizable improvised music scene, or a few of them, like London with both the Spontaneous Music Ensemble and Brotherhood of Breath,” he wrote. “And they all had international contacts and were sharing with each other. So, the originality of these approaches, and the mutual respect, encouraged the exchange between countries and scenes and the musicians and their supporters took the initiative to made it happen.”

As for his own methodology towards, as shown in this piece, the variety of musical situations in which he has taken part, Gorter spoke both simply and profoundly: “From the beginning I played both free improvisation and tunes based on chord changes. Learning on stage was an option in the ‘60s, which sometimes led to embarrassment but more often to improvement. My approach is: first try to play what you hear, then figure out what others call it (= music theory), then apply that to play better what you hear and so on. Nowadays much education starts on the second step ...”

items._cn_summary: 本文详细回顾了荷兰低音提琴手Arjen Gorter的职业生涯。他自1975年起长期担任Willem Breuker Kollektief乐团的贝斯支柱，与鼓手Rob Verdurmen共同支撑Breuker复杂而颠覆性的作曲结构。Gorter的演奏之路并非科班出身，从手风琴、尤克里里到低音提琴，他在阿姆斯特丹阁楼上的即兴摸索中找到了自己的乐器方向。文章追溯了他1966年与Breuker首次合作录制的经历，以及他与德国自由爵士萨克斯手Gunter Hampel的合作记录。Gorter的音乐扎根于欧洲即兴传统，其沉稳的低音线为先锋作曲提供了结构基础，同时也参与了1960年代末的荷兰自由爵士场景建构。文章通过对Gorter早年生活与演奏经历的梳理，展现了一位欧洲先锋爵士低音手如何在大型集体即兴乐队中扮演不可替代的基石角色。

items.body:
This column is a loose gathering of recordings – two duos, two quartets – that might define a certain frontier, a degree of meaning in improvised interactivity spreading over 12 years. At times, the combination of close listening and simultaneous writing (the only way I can find to describe this music) results in verbal collisions that may be elusive in meaning, but they may also legitimately represent some of the transformative complexity and overlapping visions arising in these works of essentially collective invention. Though one of these recordings is more than a decade old, they may represent a kind of perpetual edge.

Certain musics can pass through walls of custom, identity, and meaning, assuming unknown shapes, escaping any strict verbal denotation, meaning becoming at once plastic and ineffable. Such music cannot be analyzed or described successfully, such failed exercises, however, perhaps contributing to both its mystery and its beauty, music that might suggest a hymn from an unknown culture, possibly disappeared, to an unknown deity, possibly deceased. In collectively improvised music, the role of the listener is paramount: assembling, collecting, composing ... At the same time, however, no interpretation is more privileged than another. These particular recordings are by musicians who can create dreams in sound. Some will imagine mills or factory floors, tuned to and amplifying unimaginable inventions of human industry. Empathy contributes a mutating, transformational soundscape. These are musics that create uncommon space.

Die Dritte Ebene (45 rpm LP, NiVuNiConnu, nvnc-lp062) by Emilio Gordoa and the late Sven-Åke Johansson might initially seem exotic. Ultimately, it’s not. It’s work of perfect transparency, that is, a view of whatever one hears as the other side of anywhere. The cover offers two titles, DIE DRITTE EBEN or EL TERCER NIVEL, “the third level,” in German or Spanish, with each phrase written with the “E”s written as reversed 3s. The phrase arises in Gordoa’s brief description appended to the Bandcamp page: “We were discussing how our music moves as if in parallel lines, and how after a while something third will emerge from it, almost like a ghost. It is something I find almost mystical: how this third level manifested itself in our playing without us thinking about it.”

Reminiscent of Johansson’s previous NiVuNiConnu release, Tea Time, with Nicholas Bussmann and Yan Jun, the music hints at Erik Satie’s Furniture Music, somehow constituting a radical background music that enhances consciousness, the special resonance of repeated materials creating a trance-like, near-ecstatic state, a reflective consciousness that rises between the parts created by Johansson and Gordoa, illuminating as well as hypnotic. Die Dritte Ebene, from August 26, 2023, points to an ineffable quality – a kind of trance, a kind of lift, a spectral point of attention that is produced in a listener’s collaboration with the close echoes, tight resonance and metallic rattle of Johansson’s snare, the reeds of his accordion, and the glassy ring of Gordoa’s vibraphone, glowing like light in sonic form. The shared insistence and simultaneity of Johansson and Gordoa’s work consistently expands what is essentially a minimalist musical environment, concluding with a strange abstraction of accordion and vibraphone that might suggest a kind of musical haunting.

Nate Wooley and Seymour Wright recorded About Trumpet and Saxophone in 2012, appearing on the Fataka label in 2013. While that release was unquestionably radical, its forthcoming successor, recorded in 2025, About Saxophone and Trumpet (Relative Pitch) takes a very different initial tack, opening with a deconstruction of the romantic ballad “The Midnight Sun,” composed by Lionel Hampton and Sonny Burke in 1947, recorded initially as an instrumental, with sufficient melodic grace to have lyrics later added by Johnny Mercer, spurring recordings by June Christy, Ella Fitzgerald, and Carmen McRae. Here the melody is clearly audible through a series of gasps, honks, and shattered, incomplete phrases, a nod to tradition that rapidly expands, becoming increasingly inclusive.

There follows “Experiment Four,” an extended dialogue which includes some of the strangest sounds ever emitted by saxophone and trumpet, often coming from very different positions in the sound spectrum. The fourth track, “Untitled,” is genuinely conversational, though the conversation is conducted in assorted bleats and blasts. Each musician is repeatedly triggered by the other’s material, whether pinching their sound inward, or adapting a radical extroversion. Music here will stand in for complex human relationships and perceptions, a sound store evolving to mark the impact of events in one’s daily life, worlds for which artists have long been refining their techniques and perceptions. As our descriptive apparatus daily fails before global events, our key artists stretch the elements. In that sense, call it modern syntactical practice or a soundtrack to Guernica, but the expressive range in which Wooley and Wright here operate seems perfectly in keeping with the daily news. Meanwhile, the inner tunings and sustained tones, even their matching fast vibratos suggest the development and synergy of an expressionist language. Sudden shifts will swiftly resemble elegant balladry of yore, echoes of that “Midnight Sun.”

While the Wooley/Wright duet recalls Fataka, Trevor Brent’s remarkable label – “‘dedicated to releasing recordings of small group and solo improvisations with a particular interest in situations where a common musical language has not yet fully emerged” – has become active again, releasing Parallels & Diagonals by a quartet from the label’s earlier period, 14th July 2014 at Cafe Oto, in which Wooley and Wright appear in a quartet with two percussionists active since the dawn of English free improvisation, Paul Lytton and Eddie Prévost. Contrary to Brent’s explanation of the label (and a genuine generational difference: the percussionists had discographies before the wind players were born), the four musicians seem so closely attuned – each a genuine spontaneous composer – that they sound like they might have had a long history together. Parallels and Diagonals is 12-year-old music, but it sounds like it might be recorded next year.

The opening track, the extended Parallel A, sounds like a machine shop that has discovered free improvisation, shifting dramatically after a passage of silence shortly after the 15-minute mark. The sounds suggest a light roll on a kettle drum, a brush on a cymbal, the sound of air pushed delicately through a trumpet. This notion of interiority marks the collective passage of these musicians, finding a terrain at once both barely imagined and yet a defining part of the human condition. In Diagonal A, fundamental gestures, like air squeezed through a metal tube, take on their own significance, behaving like Buddhist mudras, invoking fundamental gestures and symptoms of human life, murmurs, signs, abrasions. Diagonal B’s rapid actions and continuous overlapping suggest activity so closely attended by the musicians that it might follow a score in which the pauses might be carefully accounted, floating among a delicately bowed cymbal, other sounds that cannot be identified, and some that shimmer around audibility.

foam and mesh (Fundacja Słuchaj Records) by the B:A:N:S BAND is the work of pianist Sophie Agnel, saxophonist John Butcher, bassist Pascal Niggenkemper, and percussionist Ståle Liavik Solberg, recorded at the 2024 ArtAct Festival in St. Johann, Austria. While it’s the only grouping here with a conventional instrumental grouping, the orientation of the musicians will ensure that there is nothing resembling convention in the ways that the instruments are utilized.

foam and mesh I is clearly the main event, a 35-minute dialogue in which four of the most skilled spontaneous composers put together a dense weave of sonic events, with nothing predictable, yet everything interlocking. Tension curves are developed with astonishing power, each member of the quartet seemingly pursuing a unique and independent path, yet everything contributing to an astonishing rhythmic taffy-pull in which every part contribute to a compound and original overall momentum. This complex relationship will sustain through numerous group movements, whether slow balladic ruminations with isolated knocks and flurries or a sudden tense wedding of trembling oscillations, all four musicians regularly finding distinct timbres. The relatively brief foam and mesh II initially foregrounds Agnel’s piano, her focus initially on brief, isolated, tight-knit clusters with abstract flurries from Niggenkemper’s bass and the randomizing knitwork of Liavik Solberg. When Butcher initially enters on soprano saxophone, the random patterns generally coalesce into a continuous stream of different rhythms and complementary densities before the work’s ultimately gradual disappearance.
items._cn_summary: 乐评聚焦四张即兴录音作品，横跨十二年，探讨集体即兴中的聆听与共写关系。文中以墨西哥裔打击乐手Gordoa与已故瑞典即兴传奇Johansson的二重奏专辑为核心展开。两位演奏者以平行的方式展开创作，在反复中催生出第三重维度——一种幽灵般的共生态。文本类比Erik Satie的家具音乐，认为作品呈现一种激进的背景音乐特质，重复材料的共振营造出恍惚与近入迷的状态，意识在双方音色之间升腾，既有催眠效果又具照明功能。整体乐评将即兴创作视为一种梦境的构建，邀请听众主动参与意义拼贴，不存在任何优先解读。评论将集体即兴音乐的开放性、不可言说性与神秘感作为核心议题，文笔具有较高的诗性与思辨深度。

items.body: Phantom Limb’s soundtrack imprint Geist im Kino is launching a new series entitled Imaginal Soundtracking on June 19. Contemporary musicians have been invited to re-score existing film pieces, with the purpose of bringing into the limelight lost or otherwise forgotten works and presenting different artistic takes on the film. In this edition, a quartet takes on the award-winning animation There Will Come Soft Rains, a 1984 film by Nazim Tulvakhodzayev which was based on the short story by Ray Bradbury, which in turn refers to a 1918 poem by Sara Teasdale, in which mankind is threatened by war. The poem also speaks of nature’s resilience, thriving once again after destruction, and after our last footsteps have been erased. Despite being written over a century ago, the poem has more than a sliver of significance in the modern era, and its ongoing relevance is quite a shock to the system. Masaaki Yoshida constructs his piece around a lonely piano and a steady metronomic click, retaining the original voice of the robot in the film to send the piece back in time and to give it a padding of authenticity, while gentle chords revolve around it, flowing freely and in stark contrast to a robot’s mechanical stutters. Quiet, sombre, and touching, the piece reflects on and walks among the debris, devastation, and stillness after a nuclear holocaust; some kind of peace even in the death of things. Lakker, Rully Shabara, and Dylan Henner bring their compositions to the record, too, but perhaps the most striking aspect of There Will Come Soft Rains is the diversity on offer, as well as the differing interpretations from the respective artists. Even though it’s the same film, the musicians have provided their own individual takes and thoughts. Electronic duo Lakker inject the music with venomous synths and complex layering which sync up with the climax of the film. Rully Shabara is the vocalist for the experimental Indonesian duo, Senyawa, and his interpretation is sculpted from a bedrock of drone and unique vocal arrangements. Dylan Henner’s track is also surprising, rephrasing and rearranging the robot’s voice until it represents something more malevolent and devilish, and the music never escapes from its doom-like feeling, which is just the kind of harmonic Imaginal Soundtracking Vol. 1: There Will Come Soft Rains was looking to hit. Imaginal Soundtracking 1: There Will Come Soft Rains by Masaaki Yoshida, Lakker, Rully Shabara, Dylan Henner www.phantomlimblabel.bandcamp.com

items._cn_summary: Phantom Limb旗下厂牌Geist im Kino推出Imaginal Soundtracking系列，邀请当代音乐人为被遗忘的影像作品重新配乐。首卷以1984年动画短片《There Will Come Soft Rains》为蓝本，影片改编自雷·布拉德伯里同名小说，灵感源自莎拉·蒂斯代尔1918年的同名诗歌，探讨战争毁灭后自然复苏的主题。吉田正明的作品以孤寂钢琴与节拍器般的机械声响为核心，保留原作机器人声音素材，营造废墟中的宁静感；双人组Lakker以毒性合成器与复杂层次配合影片高潮；Senyawa主唱Rully Shabara以人声实验与drone构建声景；Dylan Henner则将机器人声音重塑为更具威胁感的意象。多元诠释赋予同一影像截然不同的艺术生命，跨越实验电子、人声即兴与当代古典的边界。

items.body: Echo �it could be named for the Greek goddess who lost her voice, just as Chandra has lost hers to illness. Or more prosaically, it could be the memories of past performances. Whatever the inspiration, Chandra has said that this is very likely her final album. What a stupendous way to bow out. Echo by Sheila Chandra For someone who spent the first several years of her career as purely a studio artist, she proved herself to be more than adventurous when she took to the stage. Not just for the beauty of her singing, although that�s in evidence throughout, but for the surprises she could pull, as in the three hugely demanding �Speaking In Tongues� pieces here, where the relentless pace as she imitates the percussive patterns of the tablas are enough to cause whiplash. For many it was their introduction to konnokol , most often a way of teaching the rhythms, but more than powerful enough to stand alone. Live performance proved to be a reinvention for her, completely alone on stage, and the trio of albums she recorded exploring drones gave the chance to showcase her imagination and talent, the world of a pioneering artist with an individual vision. It was far from her beginnings in the early 1980s, although she revisits that teenage self on �Ever So Lonely/ Eyes/ Ocean,� transforming a pioneering Anglo-Asian pop fusion into a breathless spiritual experience. Echo by Sheila Chandra As a singer, Chandra was one to quick to spot the similarities between musical cultures, evidenced here in �Lament Of McCrimmon/ Songs of the Banshee,� where her voice soars over the subtle, grounding anchor of the drone to connect the Scottish Highland with the Indian subcontinent. It�s a lush reminder of how delicious Chandra�s singing voice was, and how much poorer the world is now medical problems have robbed us of it. For her, solo truly did mean solo � no band to back her and fill out the sound - and that produced inevitable challenges. Yet nothing here sounds empty or incomplete. The drone gave all she needed, while her vocal lines wrapped around the listener. Echo by Sheila Chandra The final track here, �The Blacksmith� was one she performed with the Imagined Village tour in 2007, making for a solemn, sad parting from the stage. Her final performances came in 2011. For those who never had the chance to see Sheila Chandra perform live, a small figure alone, commanding any stage, this is the next-best thing, with excellent sound quality and her towering presence. It�s an experience to cherish over and over. Chandra has reinvented herself again ( check her website ), but the Echo of her voice will reverberate for many years to come. Find the artist online. items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. items._cn_summary: Dorothy Moskowitz与作曲家Paladino及诗人Ferrari合作的专辑《Songs of Compassion》收录十一首作品，呈现出鲜明的反主流倾向。乐评指出音乐以钢琴为核心，穿插弦乐、木管、合成器泛音与金属音色，常以非对位相位方式叠加，拒绝传统功能和声进行，接近Steve Reich与Philip Glass式的极简与循环逻辑。Moskowitz的演唱被形容为意识流式的旋律展开，弱化旋律预期以服从歌词语义。歌词层面兼具时政批判与哲思冥想，《Pale Wanderer》与《Charlottesville》等曲目延续1960年代抗议歌曲传统，触及威权主义协作机制等议题。整体呈现出学院派当代作曲与实验人声跨界融合的特质。

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items._cn_summary: Tako Toki 乐队的第二张专辑以自制乐器为核心特色，他们用零碎杂物亲手打造了众多非常规乐器，包括低音号管、葫芦号、厨房号等，音准与音色在专业录音下表现出色。乐评追溯了几首代表作品的风格来源：'Yinitza' 呈现克莱兹默传统配以欢笑单簧管与巴松，'Le Cuenta' 融入库姆比亚元素并由横笛主导，标题曲则裹挟非洲节拍的木鱼、摇铃与马林巴琴，'Ambiguidade' 转向桑巴风格，'Aksum' 则描绘出中东迷幻色彩。评论指出乐队在选材与曲目风格之间高度契合，演奏者展现出扎实的即兴功底。整体专辑在文化融合与DIY美学之间找到平衡，既庆祝人类对节奏与旋律的普遍热爱，也提醒人们音乐不依赖昂贵乐器即可成立。

items.body: The six members of Warp Records' Providenza Ensemble will have their works performed by Sinfonietta Cracovia in a show presented by Unsound Loraine James and Puce Mary are among six artists who've produced new orchestral works to be performed at London's Barbican next year. Scheduled for 24 January, the Unsound-presented event will see Sinfonietta Cracovia, the official orchestra of Kraków, perform new pieces by Warp Records' Providenza Ensemble, which comprises James, Mary, Mabe Fratti, Clarissa Connelly, Kelman Duran and Mark William Lewis. Each piece lasts 10 minutes, and was produced to be performed by a 30-string orchestra while the six artists took part in a residency at the Corsican agricultural site Providenza. items.body: Review by meurdhek — We are dealing here with a genuine little zeuhl gem, for which Alain Lebon from Soleil Zeuhl can never be thanked enough for having rescued it from limbo, and which is bound to stir a few emotions.The listener is completely immersed in a zeuhl cauldron, with the sometimes strange yet very pleasant impression of hearing an unreleased tape from Magma's best years. The sound of Carmina, apart from a few forays into soprano saxophone and vibraphone, is very close to that of peak Magma from 1973?74.The group never repeats itself, offering ideas that are each more Magma-esque and zeuhl-driven than the last. This will undoubtedly delight fans of zeuhl music, but it also has the drawback, in my view, of slightly disorienting the listener, who may search in vain for a guiding thread within this very rich and ambitious music.One gets the impression that the band makes it a point of honor never to repeat itself and to constantly surprise the listener. Ideas come thick and fast at a sustained pace, and none is ever truly developed or explored, as the music quickly moves on to something else without any real connection between them.
items._cn_summary: 这是一张纯正的 zeuhl 小众佳作，由 Soleil Zeuhl 厂牌的 Alain Lebon 从遗忘中抢救出来。乐队以 Magma 1973-74 年巅峰时期的声响为根基，辅以女高音萨克斯与颤音琴点缀，构建出一个浓烈的 zeuhl 熔炉氛围。整张专辑构思丰富且雄心勃勃，乐句层出不穷、创意密度极高，每一段都比前一段更贴近 Magma 的美学。然而，评论者指出乐队刻意避免任何重复，试图持续给听众带来惊喜，导致想法虽多却未被充分展开，乐句之间缺乏明确的逻辑线索，听众可能在密集的素材中失去方向感。这种不断变化、拒绝发展的特质既是其魅力所在，也是其潜在弱点。对于 zeuhl 与前卫摇滚的深度爱好者而言，这是一次纯粹而忠实的类型沉浸体验。

items.body: Review by alainPP — 1. Intro (Mafar) featuring local vocals, a melancholic guitar sound worthy of Anathema, a melody reminiscent of the *The Persuaders!* theme, and stereo keyboards undulating between the speakers. Elegance, abstract Oriental rock, traditional instruments?in short, a perfect soundscape evoking life in a land that symbolizes religious massacres.2. "Nsina El 'Inwan" follows?a sad, intimate ballad driven by piano and a resigned-sounding guitar; Jeries' vocals demonstrate how a voice, when well-integrated into a tune, enhances the track without stifling the melody.3. "Min El Nar Khayfen" features crystalline keyboard work answering a sparkling guitar, with a touch of vintage organ. Philippe launches a killer guitar solo?a moment suggesting that peace is actually possible.4. "Esma' O Shouf" shifts into new-wave/darkwave mode; the rhythm guitar starts with a 60s "gangster" vibe before drifting into an 80s Marillion style, then moving toward the new-millennium sound of Riverside?fabulous. And let's not forget Raji's organ, which melts the heart; in short, it's great to rediscover them and dive back into their music.5. "Fatah 'Eneih" follows, built on a plaintive organ and guitar interplay. It has a sluggish start, then builds into a crescendo of incredible tension that wanders off into dreamlike prog, flirting with black/heavy/prog metal. Marwan's bass rides a Pink Floyd wave before washing up against a jazzy piano; the prog sound drifts along with an austere heavy riff and a haunting, persistent keyboard line. Never a dull moment.6. "Ana Malet" features a groovy, grunge-tinged riff and vocals worthy of the Sex Pistols?throwing caution to the wind: where are they headed? In any case, it's delightful to see this fusion of styles. Just as I'm settling in, the thunderous 80s-style sax from Jeries pulls us back into mainstream rock. A touch of melancholic guitar?reminiscent of Anathema?and I'm hooked.7. "El Leil Bhal 'Oyoun" returns to the Mafar sound?a welcome shift. It's a bouncy alternative track, driven by distant, heavy guitar notes. A flirtation between metal and dark rock, with the sax magically tying it all together. A track that shines thanks to its build-up and that melancholic guitar?it's a real thrill for me?leading into a soaring finale that veers into metal for that massive sound.8. "Sada" follows, pulling the same trick: a restrained, metallic guitar riff punching through against a backdrop of ethereal piano. The Anathema vibe keeps coming back to me; the piano outro, gently picking out its final notes, is simply admirable.9. The true "Outro" arrives, blending synth, violin, and melancholic guitar, all bolstered by a rich, melting organ?pure listening pleasure.An album to help you live?almost as if nothing were wrong?in this dehumanized territory; a little music to help you survive.

items.body: There is a particular kind of youthful ambition that treats a synthesizer’s limitations as somebody else’s problem. If the arrangement feels crowded, another drum track might settle the argument; if the equipment begins to struggle, perhaps it needs to be programmed harder. Baltimore’s Pygmy Children remember their earliest recordings with the affectionate candor of two people who have since learned exactly what they were putting their machines through. More than thirty years later, those experiments are getting a fresh listen. Out now through Re:Mission Entertainment, Malignant: Redux revisits the electro-industrial duo’s 1994 debut album, Malignant, and the preceding 1993 EP, Facedown. Released October 2, the collection brings brothers Pete and Brian Roper back to the recordings that introduced them to the American industrial underground, with the digital edition collecting both releases in full. Originally recorded at Hit and Run Studios in Rockville, Maryland, with engineer Steve Carr, the material has received its first official remaster from Jeff Mortimer at JM Mastering. Brian Roper supplies the Redux artwork, completing a return to a period when the duo’s appetite for dense arrangements regularly outpaced the resources at their disposal. The brothers describe those sessions with refreshing frankness: “Admittedly, the record sounds pretty raw. We were novices trying to create something multi-layered and frenetic, working with what we had and probably not fully knowing what the hell we were doing, just going for it. Some of the synths were being pushed to the point of voice exhaustion, while multiple drum tracks pounded away simultaneously. Looking back, some editing was probably in order, but the intention was always there. We may not have hit the target exactly, but the aim was definitely there.” That willingness to admit the excess is part of the appeal. Their account describes two musicians learning through accumulation, pursuing an idea until the equipment itself began to object. The early titles suggest a similarly restless approach: Core moves between Resistance and Meltdown, while Facedown appears in Reflex, Manic, Bootstamp, and Dead versions across the digital collection. Even the track listing seems reluctant to leave an experiment alone. For Re:Mission founder Wes Turner, the release also carries a personal connection. Pygmy Children helped shape his taste in dark electronic music during the 1990s; three decades on, his label is releasing both their new work and these formative recordings. Turner now gets to put the records that helped educate him back into other listeners’ hands. Listen to Malignant : Redux below: Malignant : Redux by Pygmy Children Pygmy Children first surfaced with Facedown on Noname/Noslogan Productions, following it with Malignant before moving on to Deconstruct, released by Cleopatra in 1995, and Low Life Dream, issued through Sub/Mission Records and Out Of Line in 1998. After years away, the brothers returned in 2025 through Re:Mission with Coincidental Strategies, accompanied by singles including I Have No Name and Signal Unknown. Their recent single Proof in Lies, which we covered in August, leads their forthcoming fifth studio album, Into The Silence. With new material underway, Malignant : Redux offers a timely return to the duo’s beginnings. The brothers can now afford to smile at their early excesses, though the synthesizers they used back then may still be entitled to an apology. Malignant : Redux is available digitally and on CD via Re:Mission Entertainment. Order here or find additional listening options here. Digital edition: Both Malignant and Facedown in full, comprising 16 tracks. Limited digipak CD: An edition of 100 copies, containing Malignant plus Fear, the B-side from the Facedown EP, with the digital edition included. Three-CD autographed bundle: Malignant : Redux alongside autographed original pressings of Malignant and Facedown, plus the digital edition. Limited to 25 bundles, with US shipping only. Malignant : Redux digital track listing: Shock v3.1 Xero (Absolute) Eye Core (Resistance) Mantra (Subliminal) Origin Propaganda Facedown (Reflex) Red E/E/G File Regarding… Facedown (Manic) Facedown (Bootstamp) Facedown (Dead) Fear Core (Meltdown) Follow Re:Mission Entertainment: Bandcamp Facebook Instagram YouTube Bluesky Threads The post Baltimore Electro-Industrial Duo Pygmy Children Revisit Their Earliest Recordings on “Malignant : Redux” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.
items._cn_summary: Pygmy Children 由兄弟 Pete 和 Brian Roper 组成，这张重制专辑将 1994 年首作《Malignant》与 1993 年 EP《Facedown》合并再版，由 Jeff Mortimer 进行首次正式母带处理，Brian Roper 亲自操刀封面设计。回顾这些早期作品时，乐队坦承彼时作为新手，痴迷于层叠堆砌与密集编排，合成器被推至极限，多轨鼓机同时重击，整体听感粗糙生猛却充满笨拙的野心。Re:Mission Entertainment 厂牌创始人 Wes Turner 九十年代受其影响，如今将这些影响其审美的早期录音重新推向听众。专辑多版本曲目结构体现出反复实验、不肯放过任何想法的态度，是一份来自美国工业地下场景早期声音的档案性回顾，呈现了数字时代之前的模拟电子工业之声如何从过度中摸索成型。

Economy of Movement arrives as five cuts of seriously diverse breakbeat chicaner
items.body: With Economy of Movement, Antipodean breakbeat pioneer Social Sport delivers five restless, shape-shifting cuts where fractured rhythms, heavyweight bass and psychedelic atmospheres turn the breakbeat tradition into something fiercely alive and forward-moving. Five cuts of seriously diverse breakbeat chicanery Economy of Movement by Social Sport   Antipodean breakbeat pioneer Social Sport knows what time it is. Economy of Movement arrives as five cuts of seriously diverse breakbeat chicanery, ranging across the territory occupied by beats that have escaped the tyranny of the 1 and 3. Because that, essentially, is the point: breakbeat breaks the line. Kicks bounce and lurch, snares and claps shuffle, hi-hats stammer and skitter, creating pace, tension and the possibility of movement in the spaces between expectation. Mr Sport understands these theatrics and deploys them with integrity and valor, honoring the traditions and foundations through which creator, creativity and the creative œuvre continually collide. “Inflow” opens with serious intent. Kicks move through silver atmospheres of mountain mist and textural haze, summoning elemental forces and earthly gravitas. “Life” then takes the Amen break on a tangential excursion, all aplomb and swagger, building rolling thunder from didgeridoos and chopped vocal commands. There’s something here that, to my ears at least, accidentally invokes the gods of FSOL’s “Papua New Guinea.” Not pastiche. Not homage. Something more interesting: an apparently necessary Occidental parallel evolution. Grit and grift rendered kinetic :: “Movement Economy” introduces stop-start rhythms and female vocal fragments into a 2-step-adjacent landscape of spring-loaded didges and ticking-time-bomb mood swings. Dark? Perhaps. But I don’t really read darkness here as darkness. I read power. Necessity. Seriousness. Grit and grift rendered kinetic. Tight and sick as one. “Still Working On It” brings the archetypal breakbeat throwdown: reverbed 303, filtering synth tapestries and enough dancefloor adjacency to make the whole thing twitch. It’s a proper closer, exiting with a kablamo and the brand-new stallion hoofs of badassery. Then LOIF gets involved, reworking the title track by diving beneath its surface and finding more room in the apparent darkness. The bottom end comes forward, the drums sharpen, and the bass assumes a more pronounced riff-like presence. Above it, silver clouds of smog and illumination hover while acid swirls stripe the walls with psychedelic color. It’s a redub, a reroute and a conversation with the original. More importantly, it completes the circle: five tracks that collectively reveal the specificity of an artist’s particular lens, and the possibilities that emerge when movement is allowed to escape its economy. From the other side of the globe, I see you.​ Kudos. The work is superb. Economy of Movement is available on Steeplejack. items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — This group of Finnish Vikings offers a fascinating blend of styles; they look and sound the part during live performances and draw upon Renaissance elements, not only in their compositions but also in the instruments they play. At the same time, they navigate the realm of hard rock with ease, channeling a raw savagery and boundless, spirited energy that permeates their music, extending all the way to the cover art of Susien Y�-Delirium Lupus.Kaisa Saari sings in her native tongue; alongside the distorted guitar, the sounds of a baroque viola and a traditional Viking lyre emerge in "Nostakaamme Malja," while "Muistanko V��rin" showcases Saari's soprano vocal talents. The violin, mandolin, sitar, and accordion infuse sweetness and depth into the raw power of the electric guitar and drums, creating a perfect symbiosis. It concludes like a song from a mystical forest set in the modern age, where classical elements filter through the branches of towering pines to reach a darkness that light would otherwise never penetrate.Kuninkaan Pidot leans more heavily on classical influences; amidst an acoustic soundscape of guitar and violin, it evokes the late-70s folk era of Jethro Tull, until Tarujen Saari shifts toward psychedelia, as if alcohol were flooding that ancient feast for the senses. The lyrics are an adaptation of a very old traditional British ballad known in English as "King Henry." The song highlights that appearances can be deceiving and that generosity, kindness, and genuine courtesy in the face of the unknown are rewarded with great blessings."Musta Sunnuntai" is a beautiful, powerful instrumental that also brings to mind Amon D��l II. There are also moments of relaxed introspection that evoke Scandinavian winters, possessing a cinematic quality ranging from Nordic noir to Bergman films. Armed with violin and accordion, they create a warm atmosphere that melts the snow; what might initially seem cold or aggressive turns tender, like a hearth glowing in the night.The violin arrangements are progressively symphonic in Palatynen laulu, not to mention the accelerated hard rock that also embodies Celtic tradition with electric guitar riffs in Kunungatar Kristiina.Rumpua ly�k�� kuninkaalle proposes a different atmosphere, reminiscent of those slow blues of Janis Joplin and Big Brother & The Holding Company, making it mystical with some jazzy, yet magical, percussion, making Summertime something dense and completely different. Guest musician Jaakko Rajakisto plays the bagpipes on "Hovitanssi." As "Hemminki Ja Tunturin Noita" plays, one cannot help but notice the unstoppable convergence of progressive power and ethnic harmony, embodied by that violin, recalling certain moments from Curved Air; Kaisa Saari channels the energy of Sonja Kristina across the musical spectrum, while the spirit of Daryl Way is present in Marja Tuhkanen.The surprises keep coming, notably the powerful chorus of "Susien Y�", which carries a most welcome Renaissance-style darkness. The ceremony could only culminate in a moment of delicate, subtle, and epic ecstasy, immortalized in the song "W�in�n viikate."

items.body: Review by DimitrisTheHead — There has been a big amount of albums that came before the King Crimson debut album "In court of the crimson king", that helped the shaping of the genre we call progressive rock. But it was this album that made waves and set the standards for progressive rock music for the years to come. The first album that it wasn't bluesy at all, but instead it was heavy and dark. The opening track "21st century schizoid man" sounds exactly like what you would expect to hear by only looking the album cover. Someone could say it sounds almost like Heavy Metal. The frantic last part of the song leads to the next song "I talk to the wind", an ethereal prayer, where the band shows its' softer side. The first side of the record, closes with the timeless epic classic "Epitaph'. Simply one of the best songs ever written, generally in music. "Moonchild" opens the second side of the record and it's a spellbinding tune, with majestic sounds from Ian McDonald. The haunting last part of the song, with the distant sounds, it's the perfect prologue for the closing track of the album, "The court of the crimson king", a medieval-like epic. "In the court of the crimson king" is a cornerstone of progressive rock, and if you ask me, King Crimson never matched it. Glorious.

items.body: The Australian band Chiron is back with their latest album, a project three years in the making. Led by frontman Michael Aliani (ex-IKON) and joined by bassist Dino Molinaro (IKON) and guitarist Ivan Bullock, the band presents nine tracks plus four additional remixes. Those familiar with Chiron will hardly be surprised by the influences and style: the music is a fusion of Dark-Wave and Post-Punk. The dark atmosphere that permeates the album occasionally evokes memories of Joy Division, with a pervasive sense of darkness and melancholy running throughout. The guitar sometimes takes on a psychedelic edge, adding an interesting touch, while the synth elements provide an additional melodic dimension. Yvette Winkler (Vaselyne) was invited to collaborate on the final track. The additional remixes are far from ordinary; one of them, for instance, features vocals from the cold and charismatic Kriistal Ann (Paradox Obscur). They lean slightly more towards Electro, at times incorporating a more club-oriented vibe. Chiron has never disappointed me, and with “A Dark Beauty”, the band has once again delivered a top-notch album. Personally, however, I have a particular soft spot for the slightly heavier tracks. (Rating:8). Listen to “A Dark Beauty”: A Dark Beauty by Chiron About Chiron Chiron formed in Melbourne, Australia, in 1997, founded by vocalist Michael Aliani after he left the Australian darkwave band Ikon. The project debuted with “Eve” in 1999 on the Italian label Energeia, followed by “Slipping Away” (2005, Apollyon Records), the “Breaking Point” EP (2009) and the album “We Own the Night” (2015). A compilation, “Chiron: The Best Of”, appeared on Brazil’s Wave Records the same year. The band’s 2022 album “The Sun Goes Down” marked its move to Dark Vinyl Records and brought founding Ikon bassist Dino Molinaro back into the lineup. For “A Dark Beauty”, released 17 July 2026 through Dark Vinyl Records, the band worked as a trio of Aliani on vocals and electronics, Molinaro on bass and Ivan Bullock on guitar and electronics, with Ernie Oppenheimer producing, mixing and mastering. Guest contributions come from Vaselyne‘s Yvette Winkler and Paradox Obscur‘s Kriistal Ann on the album’s remix section, extending the darker, guitar-forward direction the band set on its previous release.
items._cn_summary: Chiron 历经三年打造新专辑《A Dark Beauty》，由前 IKON 主唱 Michael Aliani 领衔，携手贝斯手 Dino Molinaro 与吉他手 Ivan Bullock 组成三人核心阵容。专辑收录九首原创曲目及四首混音作品，整体延续乐队一贯的暗潮与后朋克融合风格，弥漫着 Joy Division 式忧郁与黑暗氛围。吉他偶尔呈现迷幻色彩，合成器旋律线为作品增添层次感。终曲邀请 Vaselyne 的 Yvette Winkler 合作，混音部分则收录了 Paradox Obscur 女主唱 Kriistal Ann 冰冷而富有魅力的声线，风格偏向电子与俱乐部化处理。专辑由 Ernie Oppenheimer 负责制作、混音与母带处理，进一步强化了吉他主导的暗黑走向。整体而言，这是一张制作扎实、氛围浓郁的暗潮作品，对偏好后朋克与电子融合的听众具有较强吸引力。

items.body: Syndey Valette I Fucking Love You Artoffact Records I Fucking Love You represents a pretty big swing for Paris’ Sydney Valette. Where his material has always leaned into the history of dignified continental darkwave, Valette has never been afraid to inject some urgency, emotion and a dollop of dry humor into the proceedings. For this record he’s kicked those instincts into overdrive, making the most lively and varied album of his career to date. It’s a tightrope to maintain his measured approach to composition and performance while also letting those qualities that have previously been around the edges take a more direct spotlight, and Valette walks it with confidence and skill. Part of the record’s personality comes from how lively and ready to go the songs sound; not minimal by any means, but not overly ornamented or overworked. Opener “Warrior” is made up of a chirpy synth lead that has an almost futurepop sound, paired with a simple kick-clap drum pattern to drive it, his grave vocals, vocoder and samples from The Exorcist to fill it out. It’s effective because it’s simple and dramatic without seeming crass, a quality shared by such cuts as “Relèves-toi” whose mute pulsing bassline is punctuated by bursts of timpani and synthesized pipes, grand and even cinematic in scope, but not crowded or excessive. And when Valette really goes for the vocal gusto on the title track’s widescreen synthpop, dropping his often grave vocal delivery for a wounded croon and yelped and shouted backing, he keeps the speedy synths and drums behind him, giving himself the push and momentum for take-off. Whether those canny arrangement and delivery choices are instinctual or the product of hours of work, they really do make I Fucking Love You the album it is. Russian language cut “Как Свеча” certainly has the gravity inherent to the language as sung, and chooses to lay back in delivering its chorus, creating a tension between its melancholic and funereal mood and its zippy tempo. In perhaps the album’s most ambitious moment, closer “No Ibiza For Mr. Valette”, he goes with a plainer vocal style and uses some of his dry humor to play off what is clearly a song of heartbreak, the song slowly graduating from simple synths and drums to lush pads. Like the rest of the album, what makes it great is how it communicates so much emotionally and thematically without needing to state anything openly, saying very little but telling us everything. Buy it. I Fucking Love You by Sydney Valette The post Sydney Valette, “I Fucking Love You” appeared first on I Die: You Die.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是巴黎音乐人Sydney Valette在暗潮传统基础上的大胆转型之作。制作上兼顾了欧陆暗潮的庄重气质与活力、情感张力和幽默感，编曲克制而不冗余，层次分明。开场曲以清脆合成器主导线搭配简约鼓机节奏，并巧妙采样《驱魔人》对白，营造戏剧化却不失分寸的氛围。法语曲目运用闷哑的低频贝斯线配合定音鼓爆发，呈现出宏大且电影化的质感。标题曲则以宽阔的合成器流行编制支撑从低沉到受伤嘶吼的人声变化，产生强烈推进力。俄语曲目在忧郁葬礼感与明快节奏之间制造张力，结尾曲则用简白人声与渐进式合成器铺陈讲述心碎故事。整体在情感与主题传达上含蓄而完整，是一张兼具可听性与艺术性的作品。

items.body: Being yourself has become a surprisingly laborious business. The photograph needs editing, the opinion needs prompting, and loneliness must be presented to resemble an enviable evening. A social media profile offers the freedom to create the person we wish we were, then puts that person to work around the clock. Before long, algorithmic approval starts behaving like a drug, desire becomes a recurring payment, and the supposedly liberated individual is checking in with the platform every few minutes. The mask has developed an excellent social life, but its owner could probably use some company. Berlin’s XTR HUMAN, the long-running project of musician Johannes Stabel, turns that predicament into a forceful EBM workout on “Fake,” shared ahead of its October 9 release through Wie Ein Gott Records. The first release in a new series, the single was recorded at Infinite Power Studios in Los Angeles, with Matia Simovich handling production and mixing. Its entirely analog construction puts the emphasis on force, repetition, and the persuasive pull of an electronic beat. “Fake” opens with a metallic bass synth line that gives its EBM groove a distinctly funky gait. There is plenty of force in the repetition, though the low end knows how to move its hips. Stabel’s vocals land with a slap, a club-driven Neue Deutsche Welle drawl carrying the rhythmic confidence and insolent phrasing of hip-hop. He makes each phrase feel physically involved in the beat, pushing the groove forward with a delivery that sounds thoroughly pleased with its own bad intentions. The synth melody brings to mind the peculiar electronic funk of Fad Gadget’s “Lady Shave,” while the track’s muscular structure shares more with the disciplined body music of fellow Mute artists DAF and Nitzer Ebb. Simovich’s production keeps those elements sharply defined: the bass has weight, the rhythm has room to work, and the melody provides enough mischief to make the machinery feel dangerously inviting. That invitation is central to the song’s themes. “Fake” confronts digital isolation, manufactured identities, and the ease with which desire becomes dependency. Profiles turn into disguises; the pursuit of recognition keeps the person behind them performing. The track’s repeated patterns give that cycle a bodily form, suggesting the exhausting business of moving constantly while getting nowhere. Stabel makes the predicament sound seductive, which is precisely how such arrangements secure our cooperation in the first place. Listen to “Fake” below: “Fake” is out October 9, 2026 via Wie Ein Gott Records. Find the single here on release day. Alongside Simovich’s production and mixing, the recording credits include assistant engineers Coleman Ketchem and Grover Greenberg, with mastering by Bonati Mastering. Johannes Stabel began XTR HUMAN in 2012, developing a project whose early coldwave and post-punk interests have expanded into industrial electronics, techno, and EBM. His rich vocal delivery gives those harder rhythms a recognizable personality, drawing together German-language phrasing, new wave melody, and the propulsion of body music. Albums such as G.O.L.D in 2021 and Schrank in 2024 established a catalogue equally interested in dancefloor movement and social criticism. Earlier this year, the Rave God EP brought ’90s rave energy into that combination, including a remix by Houses of Heaven. Stabel’s international live history includes Wave-Gotik-Treffen and Absolution Festival, alongside appearances with artists including Die Selektion, Qual, Lebanon Hanover, and She Past Away. This month’s shows include a return to Los Angeles for Substance at The Belasco, followed by Berlin’s Unterwelt Festival on Halloween. Upcoming 2026 live dates: October 8 — Denton, TX — Rubber Gloves Rehearsal Studios October 9 — Austin, TX — Cheer Up Charlies (NITE SCHOOL) October 15 — Spokane, WA — Red Room Lounge October 16 — Portland, OR — The Coffin (Halloween Fetish Ball) October 17 — Seattle, WA — The Mountain Room October 24 — Los Angeles, CA — The Belasco (Substance) October 31 — Berlin, Germany — Festsaal Kreuzberg (Unterwelt Festival) Follow XTR HUMAN: Website Facebook Instagram YouTube Bandcamp Spotify Cover photograph by Anni Porrasmäki. items._cn_summary: 柏林音乐人Johannes Stabel的长期项目XTR HUMAN发行新单曲《Fake》，由Wie Ein Gott Records厂牌于10月9日推出，由Matia Simovich在洛杉矶Infinite Power Studios完成制作与混音。整首作品采用全模拟方式构建，强调力量感与重复性。金属质感的低音合成器线条赋予EBM节奏一种放克律动，Stabel的人声呈现出俱乐部导向的新德意志浪潮风格，兼具嘻哈的节奏自信与挑衅意味。制作上参考了Fad Gadget式的电子怪趣，同时具备DAF与Nitzer Ebb式的身体音乐纪律结构。歌曲主题围绕数字时代的身份伪装与欲望的成瘾性展开，循环的节奏模式将社交媒体平台上表演性自我的疲惫感具身化，让听众在听觉上体会那种看似自由实则被困的循环。整体制作锐利紧凑，低频厚重，旋律带有危险的诱惑感。

items._cn_summary: 尼古拉斯·佩顿与布彻·布朗联手，以独特视角重新诠释迈尔斯·戴维斯《Kind Of Blue》和约翰·柯川《A Love Supreme》两张爵士史上的经典专辑，恰逢两位大师诞生一百周年之际推出。作品将放克、雷鬼、拉丁及非洲音乐元素融入爵士骨架，House风格的节拍贯穿其中。《All Blues》呈现出强烈的律动质感，《Resolution》则营造出高涨的律动氛围。虽然原作经典地位难以撼动，但此张翻唱专辑的核心价值在于探讨当下重制的必要性：通过现代演绎引导听众回溯原作，从而在对照中获得全新的聆听体验。这是一次跨越时空的对话，将传统名曲置于当代多元音乐语境中重新审视。
