items.body:
A key presence on the New York scene over the past 30 years, trumpeter, composer, arranger, and bandleader Steven Bernstein has immersed himself in such a wide array of music with his bands Sexmob, Millennial Territory Orchestra, Diaspora Soul, Universal Melody Brass Band, Spanish Fly, Blue Campfire, and the Butler-Bernstein Hot 9 that his output defies easy categorization. A former member of The Lounge Lizards and Levon Helm’s Midnight Ramble Band, Bernstein has also composed works for film, theater, and dance in addition to doing arrangements for a diverse list of artists, including Lou Reed, Lee “Scratch” Perry, Allen Toussaint, Marianne Faithfull, Linda Ronstadt, Rufus Wainwright, Darlene Love, Mario Pavone, Bill Frisell, and John Lurie. His lengthy list of sideman credits includes appearances on recent recordings by Laurie Anderson (Heart of a Dog), Roswell Rudd (Trombone for Lovers), Mostly Other People Do the Killing (Loafer’s Hollow), Antony and the Johnsons (Turning), and Nels Cline (Lovers). He also continues to perform with Ray Anderson’s Pocket Brass Band, Omaha Diner, and the Kamikaze Ground Crew.

Born in Berkeley, California, Bernstein moved to New York in 1978. By 1990 he had joined The Lounge Lizards, appearing on the group’s 1991 release Live in Berlin (Intuition). Shortly before that, in 1988 he formed the trio Spanish Fly with slide guitarist Dave Tronzo and tuba virtuoso Marcus Rojas. By 1995, producer Hal Willner, a fan of Spanish Fly, enlisted Bernstein as arranger for the soundtrack to Robert Altman’s film Kansas City, which led to collaborations on numerous other Willner projects, including tributes to Bill Withers, Doc Pomus, and Leonard Cohen, among many others.

In 1996, Bernstein formed Sexmob with saxophonist Briggan Krauss, bassist Tony Scherr, and drummer Kenny Wollesen. It remains his primary vehicle for exploring the slide trumpet, a rare instrument that he picked up in a Woodstock guitar shop back in 1977. Over two decades of recording, the group has put their singular stamp on an eclectic list of tunes by the likes of Leadbelly, John Barry, Hoagy Carmichael, Paul McCartney, Duke Ellington, Prince, Kurt Cobain, the Rolling Stones, James Brown, Count Basie, Professor Longhair, and Nino Rota. The group’s latest album, in its 20th anniversary year, is Cultural Capital, the first Sexmob recording to feature all original compositions.

From 1999 to 2008, Bernstein contributed four recordings to John Zorn’s Radical Jewish Culture series on his Tzadik label – 1999’s Diaspora Soul (featuring members of The Lounge Lizards and Sexmob), 2002’s Diaspora Blues (featuring Sam Rivers), 2004’s Diaspora Hollywood (inspired by classic film composers and West Coast cool jazz), and 2008’s Diaspora Suite (a homecoming recorded with Bay Area musicians). Each project combined traditional cantorial songs and elements of jazz, blues, and rock.

Bernstein’s Millennial Territory Orchestra debuted with 2006’s MTO, Vol. 1, which featured large ensemble interpretations of songs by Stevie Wonder, Prince, and the Grateful Dead, as well as Benny Moten and Charlie Johnson and His Paradise Band. They followed with 2008’s We Are MTO, which included renditions of tunes by Fats Waller, Don Redman, Count Basie, and the Beatles. Their 2011 recording, MTO Plays Sly, was a tribute to the music of Sly & The Family Stone and featured the late P-Funk keyboardist Bernie Worrell along with guest vocalists.

In 2012, Bernstein joined up with New Orleans piano master Henry Butler in the retro-flavored Butler, Bernstein and the Hot 9. Their critically acclaimed 2014 Impulse! debut, Viper’s Drag, featured spirited renditions of Fats Waller’s title track along with tunes by Jelly Roll Morton and originals by Butler. The restlessly creative Bernstein continues to juggle several working bands. During a recent residency at The Stone in NYC, he performed with Sexmob, Millennial Territory Orchestra, Spanish Fly, Blue Campfire, and Universal Melody Brass Band.

Bernstein’s latest album is ResoNation Trio/Ultra Resonance (Royal Potato Family). In the liner notes, Bernstein mentions being enchanted by Burning Spear’s Garvey’s Ghost (Island, 1976) back in 1981, only realizing years later that it was a dub version of Marcus Garvey, Burning Spear’s Island release from the previous year. Since then, Bernstein has wanted to record an acoustic jazz trio album and have the results remade as a dub album. The first half of the release, ResoNation Trio, features Bernstein on trumpets, Scott Colley on contrabass, and Nasheet Waits on drums. To challenge himself, Bernstein eschews his main axe (slide trumpet) for this session and instead plays regular valve trumpet, G trumpet, and flugelhorn. The second half is called Ultra Resonance and features the first session tapes remixed and rearranged in dub fashion by longtime producer Scotty Hard, who also adds various keyboards, samples, and percussion to the mix. The former date is as spartan as the latter is dense, yet the two recordings (different though they are in concept and execution), are inextricably linked. I interviewed Bernstein in the summer of 2026, shortly after the release of ResoNation Trio/Ultra Resonance.

* * *

Troy Collins: You’ve been touring with Laurie Anderson the past few years, as documented by the recently released Let X = X (Nonesuch), which features Sexmob as Anderson’s backing band. What has it been like interpreting and rearranging her tunes for Sexmob, especially since Sexmob (in)famously doesn’t typically use pre-arranged tunes and/or setlists? And perhaps more importantly, how did this particular collaboration come about and what is working with Anderson herself like?

Steven Bernstein: Playing with Laurie has been a life-changing experience. She is completely about creation, being in the moment, acting on every inspiration, trying every idea and having fun. Her work ethic is legendary. Her ability to transform an audience is mastery. So being around her and that energy is just a powerful and positive situation. Even though a “show” is basically set once Laurie has decided on it (we are touring a completely different concert, different songs, different stories, different visuals, and a different “theme”) we/she are constantly making changes. Every show day we are at the theatre by 2:00 pm (she gets there at 11:00 am to start working with the lighting director) and we run every piece, whether a new idea comes from Laurie, me, another member of the band, a random sound that makes Laurie say “What’s that? Let’s try that in ‘___’.” Every idea is entertained and often added to the show.

The story of how this all started is beautiful. I’ve been around Laurie and known her at a distance for a long time, but the first time we really worked closely was doing Hal Willner’s Leonard Cohen show in Brighton in 2004. I arranged two songs for her, “The Guest” and “If It Be Your Will.” At Hal’s memorial she wanted to do Lou Reed’s “Gassed and Stoked.” I brought an arrangement that sounded just like the record and we played it through. She turned to me and said, “that sounds great, but I had another idea, I have this new loop” and she starts activating the loop with her violin bowing. It was a very “Laurie-style” loop: rhythmic, sonic, and not in 4/4 time. Tony and Kenny just drop in and start playing. It was grooving and effortless from the first sound. Laurie ended up testing positive for Covid and was unable to play the memorial, but a week later she calls and says how much fun she had playing with us. She said, “I’ve never had that feeling playing music” and that Warners is re-releasing her records and she was thinking of revisiting her older material (which she had never done), and asked would Sexmob play with her? You know my answer.

TC: Since you mentioned him, I’d be remiss to not ask about your years working with Hal Willner. The man’s various artist projects were significant touchstones in my development as a listener. I know he was a big fan of Spanish Fly – is that how you first met? And how did you become his go-to arranger for so many of his projects?

SB: I heard Hal’s Nino Rota record the summer of 1981 while visiting back home in Berkeley. Peter Engelhart, the legendary metal percussion maker played it for me (his daughters are some of my oldest and best friends). It changed my DNA! After that it became a thing. Who is Hal Willner? Where is Hal Willner? I did Night Music with Karen Mantler in 1989. I also played with Carla Bley, Bootsy, and Allen Toussaint on that show. Hal came up to me and said that he was a fan of Spanish Fly, that he’d been coming to our gigs at the Knitting Factory (lurking in the back I’m sure). He gave me his number and said that he would love to help us in any way he could. That led to him producing the first Spanish Fly record (on Knitting Factory records). It is a great Hal Willner production. Hal and I had very similar musical loves and ideas about music, he believed in me and kept offering me amazing opportunities. That led to a 25-year relationship. He could ask me to arrange for Elton John, Bill Frisell, Nick Cave, Lou Reed, Courtney Love, Robert Altman, Marshall Allan, U2 – it was always magic and natural. When I met him, it was pre-internet, and I would keep a pad of paper next to me during our phone conversations. His references could be Ernie Kovacs, Rahsaan, Allan Ginsberg, Martin Denny, Dorothy Parker, Anne Waldman, The Three Stooges, Gregory Corso, Fellini ... I did my best to keep up and learned a lot.

TC: Talking about Willner reminds me that you’ve done arrangements for more people than I can list, and the stylistic variety of artists is staggering. I’m curious if there’s ever been any job you feel you couldn’t or wouldn’t do?

To clarify, the beautiful thing about music is that someone else can take a song that seems unsalvageable and make something new from it that the original author may not have ever suspected was possible. Having just listened to a recent interview with Bill Frisell, I was reminded of his rendition of Madonna’s “Live To Tell,” which transforms what I would consider to be a lightweight pop song into a rhapsodic epic.

You are obviously capable of the same magic, but I wonder, have there ever been offers that you’ve refused based on the material or direction that someone wanted to go with it? Have you ever encountered a song that you felt was simply unredeemable?

SB: Well, there’s a funny story from about 8 years ago, at the beginning of Trump’s 1st term. It was a slow time (as often is the case for freelance workers) and I got an email from someone about arranging/producing some songs. The guy is a Sexmob fan, knows my work with Hal, and he has written some protest songs, tells me he thinks he can get Bono to sing on them, etc. He is not a professional musician, but this is his passion. He also has a vision of a performance piece situation, where the song is played while the listener goes down the “golden elevator” and walks somewhere else. We agree to a fee and he sends me the demo. He is playing rudimentary chords on the piano, and sings one verse, one chorus – it’s about 25 seconds. I call him and ask if there is more, he says no that’s the song. I explain that songs usually have a second or third verse, maybe a bridge, but he says no this is the song. I explain to him that it’s about 25 seconds, and if he wants it to work the way he is envisioning, (going down the elevator and walking) it needs to be at least 3 minutes long. He says, “Well do that Sexmob thing.” I talk to my wife and tell her that I don’t know if I can do this and she says “I thought you said you can make music out of anything.” So, I did and it ended up very cool!

TC: Well then, the obvious follow-up question to that is – did Bono sing on it?

SB: NO. A total pipe dream!

TC: Since we’ve been talking about arranging, I assume nothing is off limits in your own bands regarding your original tunes. Are there any pieces specifically written for say Sexmob, Millennial Territory Orchestra, or Spanish Fly that don’t translate as well from one band to the other, or do you compose your pieces so that any of your bands can perform them?

SB: Each piece is written not only for the band, but specifically for the players in each band. So, there hasn’t been much crossover. There is a piece I wrote as a commission during the pandemic that I played with Sexmob and MTO, but it really worked better as an MTO piece. But the very last phrase (the kicker) of the MTO end of night theme came from a Spanish Fly composition!

TC: Let’s move on to your new album. Your latest release for Royal Potato Family, ResoNation Trio/Ultra Resonance present two very different facets of your artistry – the former title finds you playing on valve trumpet and flugelhorn (instead of the ubiquitous slide trumpet) accompanied by bassist Scott Colley and drummer Nasheet Waits, while the later features Scotty Hard remixing the trio. How did this project come about and when did you first meet and work with Scotty Hard? It seems to me your working relationship with Hard goes all the way back to the very first Sexmob album, 1998’s Din of Inequity.

SB: This project came about because of a grant from the Shifting Foundation. The idea of creating original music with the orchestration of valve trumpet, acoustic bass, and drum set has been a dream of mine for a very long time. This particular vibrational intersection is not widely used, so the unknown possibilities are vast. On a musical/improvisational/technical level it has a very specific set of challenges, and it has taken me this long to feel ready to undertake this long-held desire. Scott Colley and Nasheet were always the musicians I wanted to do this with; I have known them both a long time, and they are veteran masters of spontaneous composition. Another long-held dream has been to create a dub version of an improvisatory instrumental record. I heard Garvey’s Ghost in 1981, and it changed my DNA. Once I started making my own records, I was just waiting for the right opportunity ... and this was it. The trio record is purely conversational and in the moment; back porch music with unlimited harmonic and structural possibilities. The time spent on this record was the decades of playing and writing that preceded it. Ultra Resonance is a mirror image, in that Scott creates his pieces layer by layer, adding and subtracting sounds and rhythms – it takes weeks to build a track.

When I first started playing in The Lounge Lizards with Michael Blake on tenor, Scotty started coming to hang; he was a friend of Michael’s from Vancouver. The first session we did with him was for a Justin Warfield record on Quincy Jones’ label Qwest. It was produced by Prince Paul (I am a huge fan of De La Soul). Scotty wrote the horn chart and engineered. Scotty went on to record and produce the first four Sexmob records. I was already doing fast cuts and dropouts live, but Scotty’s mixes/arrangements shaped the sound of the band.

TC: Having just listened to Sexotica (Thirsty Ear, 2006), your collaborative effort with the production duo known as GoodandEvil (Danny Blume and Chris Castagno), I’m curious how that experience was compared to your similar efforts with Scotty Hard? How does GoodandEvil’s working method differ from Hard’s and what are your thoughts on the different outcomes?

SB: Regarding the two albums/processes – they were fundamentally different as working methods and outcomes. We went into Sexotica (which got a Grammy nomination) with the idea of creating a project that was half acoustic and half electronic. Sexmob went on and recorded all the compositions (two of them being loose jams with input from Danny Blume). Then we did a full day of overdubs with Kenny: wood percussion, metal percussion, bird whistles, and gongs. Then GoodandEvil did their magic. Some pieces skewed more acoustic, some more electronic. The idea was an even balance overall.

With Ultra Resonance Scott was given all the tracks (20 songs). The first track he made, “Titano,” was a piece that’s not on the trio record, but I felt it would be a good piece for Scotty to put his magic on. I figured he would do a “remix” of it, but he rewrote the bass line and created a brand-new piece (natch). After that it was just letting Scott experiment and follow his muse. We had mapped out a series of “zones” we wanted the pieces to be in, but everything Scotty created was totally unexpected. Part of this was the idea of intentional experimentation – on both of our parts. For me it was the idea of the acoustic record, for Scotty it was some new boxes/plug-ins that he had recently received, and the idea of not going back to his tried-and-true techniques. Also, with Sexotica I was not involved in their process, but with Scotty I would hang in the studio once the “track” was created, and was involved in arranging process (Scott claims I had 3 good ideas, I’d say more like 7.6).

As far as my thoughts on the outcomes – two singular recordings that I believe are unlike anything else in the modern recording world. I’m proud of that.

TC: Switching gears slightly (towards acoustic sounds), you’re a fan of vintage horns. I’m assuming that there are certain models you never take on tour and some that you take on the road more frequently? What are the criteria for those distinctions? And what about the slide trumpet? I’m not familiar with anyone else playing one, so where and when did you ever find one?

SB: Vintage trumpets aren’t an issue on the road. I just use the horn best suited for the music. The horn I used touring with Levon Helm was a handmade Chicago Benge from 1947. That was a horn that could project over a five-piece horn section and two electric guitars. It had amazing response and Levon could feel my beat matching his. That’s not what I need with Laurie Anderson!

Regarding the slide trumpet – I found my first horn in a guitar store in Woodstock in 1977 when I was attending Creative Music Studio. When I started Sexmob 30 years ago my old friend (and master repairman) Dick Akright in Oakland (who I met in 6th grade) built the horn I use. It’s one a kind! I’ve collected almost every brand of slide trumpet over the years, though they are not as playable as my horn.

The first horn was $25, at the time (mid-70s) and many trumpet players had one because they were cheap and easily available.

TC: Speaking of Levon Helm, what was it like working with Helm and how did that relationship come about?

SB: This is a long story. I knew Levon had been having “rent party” gigs at the barn. Tony Scherr had done some, and Erik Lawrence did as well. Levon was in danger of losing the barn, as this was a last-ditch attempt to raise some money and also make some music. Erik had invited me to play a few times, and there was a Saturday where I was available (I often did a wedding on Saturday, as I was raising a family, and those gigs paid the bills). Anyway, they mention a few songs Levon might want to do (no Band songs) and said come up early because we might rehearse. We got up there and Levon didn’t come out, so I sat with a boombox and learned a few more songs that Levon “might want to do.” It was a nice chill hang up there, and when it became clear that there was not going to be any rehearsing, I told Erik Lawrence “Don’t play what I play. You just play what you hear, and I’ll play what I hear.” That way we were both free to react to the music. We were playing with Olabelle, and Levon just walked up and got behind the drums. It was the most natural improvisation/spontaneous composition. Levon didn’t know my name, had never seen me before, just smiled at me and told me what he needed with his drum fills. It was magic, and in true Levon form, he put a song from that night on one of his CD’s. Pure improvisation – we had never met!

As far as working with him – it was some of the most magic, swinging, joyous, pure music I have ever had the opportunity to create. He taught me so much about playing in time, playing melody, playing directly from the heart to the people. He was as great and real and no bullshit and smart as you would think from his legendary status. And we had FUN. And he went from almost losing everything to winning three Grammys in eight years!

TC: Speaking of legendary performers, how did you meet pianist Henry Butler, and what was your working relationship with him like?

SB: Another long and beautiful story. In the summer of 1984, I was working with the Flying Karamazov Brothers. We spent two months doing a show at the Goodman Theater in Chicago, and then went on to do a second show at the Olympic Arts Festival in LA. When that was over, they invited me up to the Eugene Country Fair, a legendary hippie festival that was associated with Ken Kesey and the Grateful Dead family. When they asked if I’d like to join them on the Old Time New Age Chataqua tour, a traveling group of “New Vaudevillians” – musicians and environmental activists that toured small communities in the rural Northwest, camping out and putting on shows – that seemed like a better option than returning to my non-air-conditioned fifth story walk up apartment on 109th street in July.

Our first stop was our one actual “gig,” at the Vancouver Folk Festival, and we headed up there directly from the Eugene Country Fair, where we had been enjoying the kind of quality research one would associate with the Grateful Dead Community. As we entered the festival, I heard a sound I was not expecting at a folk festival – a piano player, playing and singing music that seemed like it was completely futuristic, and at the same time playing music that seemed to come from early pre-jazz America. I had never heard anything like this, and at first, I thought my ears and brain were still vibrating from my Country Fair adventures, but it was actually being played, and it was (a pre-Impulse records) Henry Butler. He completely changed my DNA and I became a fan, buying his records when they came out.

When the Kansas City soundtrack record came out on Verve records, it was a time of flowing money in the record business, CDs were selling, and I believe the Bertleman Family had bought the Verve company. In 1995 they organized a cross-country tour with the Joe Henderson Trio, Charlie Haden Quartet West, and the Kansas City All-Stars, which included many Verve artists. I was the musical director of a band that included David “Fathead” Newman, Don Byron, Nicholas Payton, Christian McBride, James Carter, Mark Whitfield, etc.

I had contracted the band but was unable to find a piano player (Gerri Allen and Cyrus Chesnut had done the movie). I contacted seemingly every pianist in NYC who would fit the bill, and none were available, and I was starting to panic. I called Hal Willner to ask his advice and without missing a beat he said “did you call Henry Butler?” And that’s how it all started.

Henry and I were kindred spirits and when the tour was over he told me we would work together again. In 2011 I was doing an “MTO Plays the Early Blues” concert at a summer series in NYC. The promoter, Jay Weisman, asked if I’d like to have Henry Butler play, and I said of course, but where is he? It turned out he had an apartment in Brooklyn, post Katrina. When the concert was over Henry called me and said we should do a show with MTO playing all of his music – that was the birth of Butler Bernstein and the Hot 9 (there were 10 people in the band). As far as my working relationship, he totally trusted my bandleading instincts and arranging, and I was always awed and inspired by the music flowing out of him.

TC: You bring up a salient point. Around the time of the Kansas City soundtrack, there seemed to be a very healthy major label interest in jazz that benefitted musicians of all stripes, even those somewhat on the fringe (James Carter, Don Byron, David Murray, etc.), which to me, evoked the pre-Young Lions era, when major labels signed post-loft jazz artists like Anthony Braxton, Arthur Blythe, and Henry Threadgill.

Much has changed since then. I’m curious what your thoughts are on that phenomenon? How have you adapted to the changing fortunes of the recording business? And what do you foresee for the future?

SB: Well, the beautiful thing is that I have been DIY since the beginning. I think the budget of the first Spanish Fly record (which was on Knitting Factory Records) was 3K, and Hal Willner produced it! I personally have never really had a record contract where I was signed and had a budget. I’ve had a few independent contracts, and records funded by public and private grants. That is the way everything is now, so it’s just the way I’ve always been able to create new things. And that’s what it’s about, creating new things.

TC: In reference to creating new things, I’m curious about your thoughts on live performance versus studio recording. Studio recordings of Sexmob often feature a fair amount of electronic manipulation and remixing, much like Ultra Resonance. What are your thoughts on the difference between purely acoustic performances versus such heavily processed and studio manipulated recordings? Do you vary your approach towards playing depending on the situation?

SB: My feeling is that once Electric Ladyland and The White Album came out, there was no turning back. Even my albums that aren’t “heavily electronically processed” (aka produced by Scotty Hard) feature mixes that are very specific, often times emphasizing certain frequencies, the same way a painter will use certain colors to draw the eye. I believe a record should be a mind-altering listening experience. ResoNation Trio is also a studio record, although one that creates a vision of an imagined acoustic experience. As far as playing, I just do the best I can when the recording light is on!

TC: Let’s go back to those early, heady days. According to your bio, you grew up in the Berkeley area and were friends with Peter Apfelbaum, with whom you regularly attended jazz gigs. There was mention of an “eye-opening gig” by the Art Ensemble of Chicago at San Francisco’s Great American Music Hall. What was it about that particular show that resonated with you?

SB: It was just seeing them live after listening to the records for two years. The magic and visceral-ness of it. There is magic that happens when you are in the room, seeing the musicians and feeling the vibrations, sharing the communion of music. We also met them that night. We were pretty heady. We went to their dressing room and banged out “Nfamoudou-Boudougou” on the door. They were certainly shocked to open the door and see two scruffy teenagers.

They welcomed Peter and me into the dressing room, and that started a relationship that continues to this day (Peter is still in touch with Roscoe). When I moved to NYC I went to see the AEC at the Public Theatre, either late 1979 or early 1980. Now when we went to shows in the Bay Area everyone was dressed hippie funky, so that’s how I showed up, probably in overalls and a t-shirt. I go backstage after the show and am totally self-conscious to be surrounded by well-dressed urban New Yorkers in Kente Cloth and immaculate jewelry. Lester opens up the dressing room door, peeks out at all the “beautiful people” and says “BERNSTEIN get in here!” closes the door, points to the table and says “you can roll a joint, right?” (I could).

TC: Now that’s funny. I certainly remember my one and only time seeing the Art Ensemble of Chicago. It was in Philadelphia, at The Clef Club. Jarman wasn’t touring with them at this point, but it was still magical, ceremonial even.

One group I regretfully never saw was The Lounge Lizards. You were a member of The Lounge Lizards in the 1990s. How did that association come about? And while bandleader John Lurie has had an unusual (to say the least) life and career path since then, I was wondering, do you still have any contact with him?

SB: I have yet another tall tale to tell. It was summer of 1989 and I was touring with Chautauqua again, the same group of people I was touring with when I first heard Henry Butler in 1984. Back then we had answering machines that you called into and used a beeper to retrieve your messages (This is pre cell phones). I was in a small town somewhere, probably Idaho or Montana, and I went to a payphone and checked my messages, and I heard a message from John’s assistant saying to call John up because he was interested in having me join The Lounge Lizards. Needless to say I was beyond excited, because The Lounge Lizards was the “Premiere Band” on the downtown scene.

I call John up and the first thing he says to me is “Do you have a suit?” The next thing he says to me is “you’re not gonna get a lot of solos.” Luckily, the tour was heading to a place of general civilization (Port Townsend) and I was able to put together a tape so John had an idea of what my playing was like, and that September I started rehearsing with the band.

I still talk with John. The most recent project we did together was working on music for his film, that was two summers ago. We did music for Painting with John, and there was an excellent and entertaining episode in season three (I believe) that featured the making of the soundtrack, which really showed the process that we use.

Early on with The Lounge Lizards I started to arrange and transcribe for John, first working on Fishing with John, which led to arranging and conducting soundtracks such as Get Shorty and Excess Baggage. Get Shorty was the summer of 1995, and John and I would spend 12 hours a day together as I transcribed his ideas and put them into notated forms.

TC: I’m glad to hear you’re still in contact with John. Speaking of the 1990s, you recorded four albums in the late 1990s to early 2000s for John Zorn’s Radical Jewish Culture series on his Tzadik label: Diaspora Soul (1999); Diaspora Blues (2002); Diaspora Hollywood (2004); and Diaspora Suite (2008). As a fan of those albums, I’m curious if you ever return to any of those tunes or arrangements?

SB: I’m glad you brought up those records. I love the Diaspora series too. Yes, it lives on. I wrote big band arrangements of some of this music for Arturo O’Farril and the Afro Latin Jazz Orchestra for two different concerts. I arranged a version of “Ani Mamin,” which I recorded with saxophones and valve trumpet on Diaspora Soul, reimagined as a tribute to Eddie Palmer and Conjunto Libre, arranged now for four trombones and slide trumpet. I learned that Barry Rogers, the architect of the New York salsa trombone sound, was raised in Brooklyn and his father and uncle sang with Moshe Kousevvitskey’s choir. Full circle New York history for you. I also recorded a version of “Cha” with Arturo and the Afro Latin Jazz Orchestra. We recorded it during the pandemic, so it's all over-dubbed. “Cha” was inspired by John Zorn’s composing for Masada, and I created an arrangement inspired by Machito. I recently revisited the Diaspora Blues music alongside Arturo O’Farrill, Anat Cohen, and a small version of the Afro Latin Jazz Ensemble. This October at the Stone I'll be premiering a duo version of the Diaspora music with Arturo O’Farrill, so the music lives on, and keeps evolving.

TC: What other musical projects or performances do you have coming up in the near future?

SB: Here are a few upcoming shows:

September 23-29: Laurie Anderson and Sexmob, West Coast Tour and Chicago October 1: Helm Family Ramble in Brooklyn October 2: ResoNation Trio at Tempo, Kingston NY October 28: ResoNation Trio at The Stone October 29: Ultra Resonance at The Stone October 30: Diaspora Special Edition with Arturo O’Farrill at The Stone October 31: Sexmob Kurt Weill Halloween at The Stone

Sexmob Live at Carambolage, Bolzano (the last night of our March 2026 European tour) will be released at the end of the year. It’s our first documentation of the “new sound” of the band with Kenny’s electro drums in the mix.

And more upcoming projects that I’m not quite ready to announce.

items.body:
There is a substantial list of attributes that sets Ran Blake apart from every other innovative pianist of the past sixty-plus years, each of which falls under one of two headings: his choice of materials and his treatments of them. The former is based on Blake’s ability to hear connections between materials for which “disparate” is an inadequate descriptor. Who else would sequence Max Roach’s “Mendacity” and “Saving All My Love for You” – or “On Top of Old Smokey” and Michel Legrand’s “Watch What Happens”? Nobody, because what Blake does is unique. He doesn’t interpret materials as much as administer an MRI, revealing the connective tissues and vital organs as vividly, if not more so, than the skeletal structure. In the process, Blake makes the familiar sound radically new.

Blake’s collaborations with singers are central to his work. The current critical consensus is that his groundbreaking work with Jeanne Lee overshadows everything since, the respective qualities of notables like Christine Correa and Sara Serpa notwithstanding. Roots & Byways circumvents the edifice The Newest Sound Around has become, primarily because Dominique Eade takes a different tact. She is not as rooted as Correa – or Lee, for that matter – in Billie Holiday, and she is not as committed to understatement as Serpa. Like both Correa and Serpa, Eade can shape a song syllable by syllable and render a highly personal interpretation. It is Eade’s palpably deep joy in singing that sets her apart, one that is not only bursting at the seams on showstoppers like the Whitney Houston megahit, but one that even seeps into noirish songs like Mingus’ “Portrait.” It is the key to her relatability and appeal, and to that of the album, as well.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑展示了Ran Blake独特的钢琴艺术与Dominique Eade的声乐合作。Blake以极具创意的选曲著称，将风格迥异的作品并置——从Max Roach到Michel Legrand，从传统民歌到Whitney Houston流行金曲——通过非传统编排揭示素材之间的深层连接。他不拘泥于传统和声或结构框架，而是以解构与重组的方式重塑熟悉曲目。Eade的演绎则以深沉而饱满的喜悦感为标志，她在逐字逐句雕琢歌词的同时，将真挚情感注入作品。她区别于其他合作歌手的特质在于那种跃动的生命力，既能在明快的热门歌曲中绽放，也能在阴郁的Mingus作品中渗透。整张专辑在Blake的实验性钢琴框架与Eade的个性化诠释之间形成张力，展现了非传统选材与情感深度并存的声乐爵士新路径。

items.body: Dau, the moniker of UK ambient musician Phil Self, is about to release his solo debut, Zed Zed. Arriving via Phantom Limb’s new sub-label imprint Spirituals, which promotes ‘high grade, emotive ambient and experimental music from emerging artists from across the world’, Zed Zed is a beautifully-crafted and intricately-woven record, utilising classical chamber orchestration and blending it with an ambient core. Self is involved in many other projects, from the UK instrumental sextet yndi halda to performing in the live band of folk-rock singer-songwriter Will Varley. Self also runs the Isolation Choir, a non-profit initiative for the elderly and the vulnerable, where musicians and non-musicians alike are invited to contribute remotely to pieced-together ensemble performances (the first video of which caught the eye of Brian Eno, who was so moved by the performance and the compassionate message behind the project that he offered his services for the second). Zed Zed features bowed guitar, reed organ, and voice, but Self also includes recordings of water bowls, falling rain, and sounds from his kitchen, which produces a warm, comfortable, and homely atmosphere, adding degrees of personality and intimacy within the familiar environment of home. The human qualities of empathy, kindness, and care are literally at the centre of the music, a point at which it can brightly shine, and it also reflects Self’s own personality, the music acting as a conduit for his inner kindness. The music unravels with patience, slowly developing and building upon itself. Perhaps most importantly, Zed Zed is free of computer processing; digital editing and computer interference is rejected. The record is entirely acoustic and proud of the fact, featuring real-time performances and nothing but acoustic instrumentation. A deep ambient heart beats within its music, which is all the more evident in the dulled harmonic resonance of its water bowl. And along with the sound of dripping water, reverberating gongs help to produce calming sensations and feelings of immense relief. With graceful movements, the music never seems to put a foot wrong. ‘Sundowning’ closes the album as an overlapping family of lean, slanting strings provide the last flares of light. Even with the sunset and its representation of ending and finality, the music’s message is one of enduring beauty, optimism, and appreciation, retaining its grace right up until its end. PSALM003: Zed Zed by Dau www.phantomlimblabel.bandcamp.com

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由英国环境音乐人Phil Self以Dau名义发行，是其首张个人全长作品。整张唱片以原声乐器为核心，刻意排斥任何电脑处理和数字编辑，全部由实时演奏完成。弓拉吉他、簧风琴与人声构成主要声部，同时大量收录水碗、雨声、厨房环境等日常声音素材，营造出温暖、私密且具有强烈家居氛围的聆听空间。古典室内乐编排与环境音乐内核相互交织，缓慢展开、层层递进，克制而沉稳。评论特别指出作品中蕴含的人性关怀——音乐不仅是审美表达，也折射出创作者自身的同理心与善意。专辑结尾曲以倾斜的弦乐收束，传达出关于终结与美的双重讯息。整体而言，这是一张在极简框架内追求手工质感与情感深度的作品。

items.body:
After the OĽUN album I reviewed enthusiastically a while back, here’s the next project, again motivated and led by violinist/fiddler/composer Ján Kružliak Jr., continuing the rapprochement, indeed embrace, between Slovakia’s traditional music and its classical music. This time it reconnects the works of classical composers who were inspired by and drew on village musics with those traditional sources and styles.
Three ensembles are involved: the Spectrum Quartett led by Kru�liak with two violins, viola and cello; Nogaband, the traditional-style quartet of fiddles, contra (chording viola) and bass that’s led by fiddler and singer Michal Noga; and the female vocal group Ulijanky, plus guest singer Simona Hulejov�.
The majority of the tracks are interpretations of works by Slovak composer Eugen Suchon (1908-1993), with others from fellow-Slovaks Ilja Zeljenka (1932-2007) and Alexander Moyzes (1906-1984), and Hungarian B�la Bart�k (1881-1945) who did a lot of his very detailed collecting of folk music in Slovakia.
In each case the sources - musicians and locations in villages across Slovakia - are credited in the notes, and these arrangements and performances reconnect with the energy and traditional vocal sound of those sources.
In no way is this an orchestra-smoothed thing; this is gutsy, brilliantly played and sung music with all the spirit, skill and technique of traditional music, from players and singers who deeply understand and inhabit it. It’s a glorious piece of work, music to luxuriate in. There’s too much richness to begin to detail, but here’s a dip into a few moments to give the flavor. The tracks all have very long titles detailing their sources, so for brevity’s sake I’ll just give track numbers.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由小提琴家/作曲家Ján Kružliak Jr.主导，延续其前作将斯洛伐克传统音乐与古典音乐交汇的探索方向。三组音乐家——Spectrum Quartett弦乐四重奏、Nogaband传统弦乐组合及Ulijanky女声合唱团——共同重新演绎斯洛伐克作曲家Eugen Suchoň、Ilja Zeljenka、Alexander Moyzes及匈牙利作曲家Bartók受民间素材启发的作品。每首曲目都标注了采集村落音乐素材的具体来源与演奏者，使当代编配与民间能量、声腔传统形成直接对话。专辑不走管弦乐化的圆滑路线，而是保留了传统音乐粗粝有力的质感，演奏与演唱均展现出对民间语汇的深入理解。整体呈现出古典框架与乡村音乐源头之间跨越时空的重新连接。

items.body:
Though this recording documents the work of thirteen of Belgium's most innovative ensembles, the real star is the Park Abbey located just outside Leuven and founded in 1129. Built and maintained for the purpose of quiet meditation, the abbey hosted the musicians who used the quiet surroundings to prepare and record their unique musical imaginings. The result is a mostly instrumental collection that mines the riches of Belgian folk and world music traditions, including Romani scales,
La Pump
rhythms, and accordion-based
bal-musette
flavors.
For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�
Despite the wide range of styles,
The Sound of the Abbey
has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. They have rendered a warm sound using the natural reverb of ancient stone provided by the project�s silent partner.
Find out more about Merodefestival.
Further reading and listening
Piet Maris and Sarah Baur talk about the artist collective Choux de Bruxelles
(Interview)
W�R x Kongero -
Songbooks Live
(Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑录制于比利时鲁汶附近的帕克修道院，由十三支比利时创新乐团合作完成，历时三年制作。乐评指出修道院的古老石质空间与宁静氛围成为音乐的隐性合作者，录音师利用天然混响营造出温暖的声场。曲目横跨罗姆吉普赛音乐、巴尔-木塞特手风琴、阿拉伯-地中海调式、巴洛克古典元素及凯尔特喉音等多种传统，融合中提琴律动、乌德琴、西特琴与曼陀林等乐器。部分作品带有即兴与冥想特质，如Airboxes使用半音阶与全音阶手风琴即兴对话，标题暗示对修道院永恒感的回应。整体虽风格多元，却因共同的灵感来源形成内在统一性，既出人意料又令人舒缓，呈现出欧洲民俗与世界音乐传统的当代交汇。

certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody o
items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. More to hear: United States of Alchemy - Songs of Compassion (Review) Dani Jan� - Vida (Review)

items._cn_summary: Alison Cotton 的新专辑延续了她标志性的模糊美学，将民谣、前卫与宗教仪式感融为一体。中提琴、簧风琴、击弦古钢琴与钢琴构成核心乐器配置，新专辑中加入鼓、贝斯与合成器，扩展了声音层次。音乐多为即兴录制，一次性完成，呈现出静谧、近乎神秘的气质。专辑也是对2024年末去世的父亲的纪念，《最后的收获》以庄严笔触追忆父亲最后一次造访他深爱的菜地，情感渗透于音符之间。作品巧妙融合中世纪圣乐、英格兰自然诗人John Clare的文本与古老民歌的回响，光与暗在旋律中交织流动，超越了传统分类的边界。

items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)

items._cn_summary: Analog Africa 厂牌发行的这张合辑聚焦贝宁传奇乐队 Orchestre Poly-Rythmo 与歌手 Antoine Dougbé 1977 至 1982 年间的合作录音。Dougbé 以双腿拍击 Cavacha 节奏著称，这种由鼓手 Belobi Meridjo 从火车节奏中提炼出的律动曾席卷 1970 年代中期刚果流行乐坛。作为伏都教信仰的实践者，Dougbé 对演奏者有严苛要求，最终只与 Poly-Rythmo 合作，留下三张专辑与若干单曲。音乐扎根于伏都教驱动的萨托与萨克帕塔传统放克，又融入古巴松的明显影响——牛铃、鼻音人声对答与紧凑重复的吉他段落清晰可辨。合辑前段曲目更直接呼应古巴元素，中后段则呈现合成器铺底、吉他带有塑料质感的高光音色，器乐在合成器织体上展开多向对话。录制年代决定了录音与乐器音色的时代特征，但音乐的根脉仍牢牢扎在 1970 年代的非洲节奏土壤中。

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio
items.label: Taragot
items._genre: experimental jazz / folk fusion / free improvisation
items._cn_summary: 这是挪威Camilla Hole Trio在延续前作科幻合成器与传统素材嫁接的脉络后，转向更为'脚踏实地'的一张作品。核心乐器为高音萨克斯，爵士影响显而易见，但三人组合刻意模糊各自的角色分工：贝斯手与鼓手并不固守节奏支撑，而是频繁参与到旋律线与即兴展开之中。开场曲取材于挪威西部的传统春季舞蹈曲调，萨克斯先陈述主旋律，随后贝斯与鼓手逐步加入对位与即兴拓展，并在尾声由萨克斯再次回归收束。模块合成器与颤音琴的叠加为传统旋律提供了新的色彩层次，使整张专辑在北欧民谣素材与自由爵士即兴之间形成持续对话，适合对跨界融合感兴趣的听众。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 古巴钢琴家Omar Sosa在意大利Fazioli钢琴音乐厅完成了一场两小时的独奏即兴录制，后期混入少量人声采样、打击乐、循环片段、田野录音和环境声响。专辑诞生于疫情封锁与个人生活的转折期，演奏拒绝预设结构，强调首遍演奏的自然性，延续爵士传统中的即兴精神。后期制作中点缀的极简音效与原声钢琴形成对照，既有冥想式的内省质地，也保留了爵士钢琴的即兴脉络。Sosa明确表示不愿被风格归类，试图在传统与现代之间找到新的路径。该作品融合了古巴音乐根源与欧洲古典钢琴传统，文章从创作背景、录音环境到艺术家哲学观念均有较深入的访谈式评述。

items.album: Recent Reviews at Chain D.L.K.

Returning to its home of Colchester Arts Centre, the event will take in a headline appearance from Mike Paradinas' µ-Ziq project, featuring immersive visuals from ID:Mora. items.body: Eight years after Bone Bame, the Paris collective return with a record named after a Cameroonian mountain that traps walkers in a dance they cannot quit. The reason they chose that story is more pointed than the sleeve lets on Somewhere in the middle of the Bone Bame touring cycle, 10LEC6 stopped being able to work. Nicole, the singer whose voice is the entire centre of the group, was served an OQTF, the French administrative order requiring a person to leave the country. The practical result was that the band could not honour festival bookings outside France. A Paris collective built almost entirely on movement, on diaspora, on rhythms carried between continents, was pinned to one territory by paperwork. It was Nicole... items._cn_summary: 巴黎集体10LEC6在首张专辑八年后推出新作，标题取自喀麦隆一座让行走者无法停止跳舞的山峰。主唱Nicole的声音构成整支乐队的核心，围绕她铺展着跨大陆迁徙的节奏脉络。专辑名背后的故事远比封面暗示的更尖锐：巡演期间Nicole收到法国行政离境令，导致乐队无法履行法国境外的音乐节合约。一个以流动、离散与跨洋节奏为根基的巴黎集体，被行政文书钉死在一国领土之内。这张专辑从这一困境中生长，将无法移动的身体所积聚的能量转化为音乐——关于边界、关于被迫静止的人如何通过节奏持续运动。整体倾向实验制作与世界节拍的交融，但因正文信息有限，对具体声响手法的展开不够充分。

items.body: Review by kenethlevine — If SCARLET THREAD wasn't conceived as one of those single guy projects with a revolving support system, it became one fast during the interval between their "Psykedeelisi� Joutsenlauluja" and "Valheista Kaunein", with personnel in flux right through the early recording sessions. Only JANI TIMONIEMI remained, but he did keep the guitar/violin/flute instrumental orientation, so this doesn't sound all that different from the jam-oriented and jazz accented debut. Perhaps a bit heavier in parts such as on "Jumalanilkkakirves" and "Levoton Sielu", this is still balanced with the pastoral woodwinds and strings. The opener kicks off with an irresistible riff but doesn't support it enough when offstage. Some of the numbers sound like they are just trying to get to the end, while simultaneously shrugging like they have no idea how to end it. Still, the KC trio era plus folk influences, particularly on the more succinct "Aatoksia Kivusta" and "Haarasilta" , make this a worthwhile 43 minutes, and worth returning to when the mood strikes.
items._genre: prog folk / jazz fusion / psychedelic folk
items._cn_summary: 这是芬兰乐队SCARLET THREAD的第二张专辑，乐队在两张专辑之间经历了频繁的人员变动，最终仅由吉他/小提琴/长笛多面手Jani Timonemi独立支撑完成。专辑延续了首作以吉他、小提琴与长笛为核心的器乐取向，整体偏向即兴化的民谣底色，同时融入了爵士和声语汇与前卫摇滚的结构感。部分曲目如《Jumalanilkkakirves》和《Levonen Sielu》稍显沉重，而田园风的木管与弦乐段落则在对比中提供喘息空间。评论指出开场曲以一段抓人的riff起势，但主体展开缺乏足够的支撑；部分曲目似乎在摸索中走向终点，既没有清晰的收束也没有明确的走向。但KC三重奏时期影响的残影与民谣元素的交织，使较为短小紧凑的《Aatoksia Kivusta》和《Haarasilta》等作品成为专辑亮点。整体43分钟的长度虽不完美，仍值得在特定心境下重听。

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — Ceiba by Temic is a fantastic progressive metal album from the newest prog supergroup, showcasing great technical melodic instrumental work and great emotional vocals from Fredrik Klemp. Taking members from The Neal Morse Band, Shining, Maraton & ex Haken keyboardist Diego Tejeida, the interplay between Tejeida & Eric Gillette's melodic shredding is very impressive and at times would even give Jordan Rudess & John Petrucci a run for their money. While there are great heavy polyrhythmic moments, the focus on melody and harmony is also potent, which really gives the band an emotional edge. A spark which could be a very bright future for the project. I'd give this a mid 8 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is Parting The Waves Inside.
items._cn_summary: 这是一张由多位知名前卫金属/摇滚乐手组成的超级组合专辑，乐手分别来自The Neal Morse Band、Shining、Maraton以及前Haken键盘手Diego Tejeida。专辑以技术性旋律演奏为核心，键盘手Tejeida与吉他手Eric Gillette之间的旋律交织令人印象深刻，在某些段落甚至可与Dream Theater的Jordan Rudess和John Petrucci相媲美。作品中既有复杂的多重节奏段落，也注重旋律与和声的情感表达，在力量感与情绪深度之间取得了平衡。作为一支新兴项目的首张作品，展现出值得期待的发展潜力。整体而言，专辑在前卫金属框架内做出了扎实而有感情的表达，但在更广泛的实验性或跨类型融合方面着墨不多。

items.body: Israeli gothic metal band Fatum Aeternum has rebuilt “P.W.Y.P.” for a streaming release, bringing the track back from their 2012 EP “The Sermon.” The self-released single went out digitally on 25 September 2026. The new version keeps the original ’80s glam-rooted guitar riff while adding aggressive male vocals, a female counter voice, cello and a full gospel choir. Where the 2012 recording leaned on social commentary, the rebuilt arrangement expands it into a more layered, theatrical gothic sound the band describes as a dark sermon. “P.W.Y.P.” is the second single in Fatum Aeternum’s renewed run of releases, following the comeback single “As Above, So Below” on 25 August 2026. That single introduced a new six-piece lineup – Steve Gershin, Evelyn Shor Gershin, Dr. Joe, Victor Grassiano, Max Datskovsky and Mark Muzykant – which also plays on “P.W.Y.P.” The track was recorded at Lodge Studios in Northampton, UK. Denis Saenko handled mixing and mastering, with additional mixing by Gershin; Tayo Olawepo arranged and recorded the choir. The band’s promotional materials cite Lacrimosa, Therion and Haggard as reference points. “P.W.Y.P.” is available to stream on Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube, Amazon Music, Deezer and SoundCloud. About Fatum Aeternum Fatum Aeternum formed in Tel Aviv, Israel, in 2006, built around Steve Gershin on mandolin, bass and vocals, alongside Ze’ev Gut on fiddle and vocals and Olga Braverman on flute and vocals. The group’s first full lineup added Ilya Surnin on drums, Dan Yoffe on guitar and Rivka Aizenberg on viola, playing a self-described “renaissance metal” blend of folk and metal. Braverman left in 2007 and Gut in 2008, staying on as a guest musician as the band shifted toward a heavier, more electrified sound. Gershin considered disbanding the group in 2009 and recorded a memorial album of earlier material instead; Evelyn Shor Gershin joined permanently around the same time, stabilising the lineup. The band re-recorded its debut album “This Dream Is Dead” several times before releasing it on CD in 2011. On 24 September 2011, Fatum Aeternum played the 12th Children of the Night Gothic Festival in Kyiv, Ukraine, its first show outside Israel, sharing the bill with Waves Under Water and Diary of Dreams. The video for “Apocalypse Now” followed on YouTube in April 2012 and aired on MTV Israel’s “Headbangers Ball” that June. The band self-released the EP “The Sermon” in September 2012, recorded at Lodge Studios in Northampton, UK, and opened for Apoptygma Berzerk the same month before going on hiatus in 2013. Gershin and Evelyn Shor Gershin rebuilt the lineup with George Falk and Igor May in 2014, releasing the single “One Bastard” that April and the maxi-single “The Pain” later the same year. The EP “The Darkest Hour” followed in 2015, then “Mass Suicide of Human Race” in 2017 and “Singing Songs of Desperation” in 2020. Fatum Aeternum returned in 2026 after a three-year gap, a pause the band’s own site attributes to health issues within the group. The comeback single “As Above, So Below” arrived on 25 August 2026 with a new six-piece lineup of Gershin, Evelyn Shor Gershin, Dr. Joe, Victor Grassiano, Max Datskovsky and Mark Muzykant. “P.W.Y.P.,” a rebuilt version of the 2012 “The Sermon” track, follows as the second single in that renewed run.
items._cn_summary: 以色列哥特金属乐队Fatum Aeternum重新构建2012年EP《The Sermon》中的〈P.W.Y.P.〉，于2026年9月25日发行流媒体版本。新版保留带有八十年代华丽摇滚根源的吉他 riff，加入更具攻击性的男声、女声对唱、大提琴以及完整的福音合唱团，将原本带有社会评论色彩的作品扩展为层次更丰富、戏剧性更强的“黑暗布道”式声音。本作是乐队重组后的第二支单曲，采用六人新阵容，并在英国Lodge Studios录制，由Denis Saenko混音与母带处理。整体融合哥特、暗黑与新古典元素，适合偏爱阴郁氛围和金属跨界融合的听众。

items.body: Three years after its 2023 singles “Purgatory” and “Lifeline,” Los Angeles futurepop act State Of The Union has released a new single, When Daylight Dies, out October 5, 2026 on Bandcamp. State Of The Union is the solo project of Johann Sebastian. On the new single, he said he hopes it “connects with you, and we look forward to sharing more music with you soon.” When Daylight Dies by State Of The Union “When Daylight Dies” is available as a digital single on Bandcamp. About State Of The Union State Of The Union is a Los Angeles electronic industrial and futurepop project fronted by Johann Sebastian, with drummer Jimmy Nimra contributing to past studio releases. The project’s prior full-length, “Impendum,” came out in 2004. State Of The Union signed to Infacted Recordings and released the digital EP “Mindless” in November 2018, followed by the CD album “Indupop” and the digital EP “Industrial Slither / Remixes” in early 2019, and the EP “Bad Flower” in 2020, all on Infacted Recordings. The project went quiet for three years before returning with the singles “Purgatory” in August 2023 and “Lifeline” in October 2023. With “When Daylight Dies,” State Of The Union returns for the first time since that pair of 2023 singles, and Johann Sebastian has signaled more music to come.
items._cn_summary: 洛杉矶未来流行与电子工业音乐人 State Of The Union 推出新单曲《When Daylight Dies》，继二〇二三年的《Purgatory》与《Lifeline》后首次回归，计划于二〇二六年十月五日通过 Bandcamp 以数字单曲形式发行。主创 Johann Sebastian 表示希望作品能与听众建立连接，并暗示后续仍会有更多音乐。文章主要介绍发行信息、艺人背景及过往作品脉络，缺少对编曲、声音设计、表演细节或作品独特性的深入评析，因此难以充分判断其艺术价值。

items.body: Silence has a talent for passing itself off as peace. Two people can share a room, exchange the necessary pleasantries, and conduct an entire argument without troubling the air between them. Inside, every withheld accusation is already gathering speed. Given enough time, even “How was your day?” can begin to sound like a contact sport. Milan quartet October take that condition onto the ice in their video for Universe. The fourth single from their debut album, Dancing Like an Idiot, out now through Waddafuzz! Records, follows the uncomfortable distance between what a relationship looks like from the outside and what its participants are putting themselves through within it. A frozen surface can conceal considerable commotion, and October have enlisted a hockey team to give those private collisions a public airing. The song itself has a supple, sophisticated swing. A rhythmic bassline brings the new wave funk of Roxy Music and Japan to mind, its firm articulation keeping the groove grounded as sustained guitar tones stretch above it. The snare lands at deliberate intervals, leaving generous space around each strike. There is a progressive streak in the arrangement, a willingness to let the instrumental passages stretch and change shape without losing the underlying rhythm. Gianluca Villa sings in a silky upper register reminiscent of Peter Gabriel, his measured delivery building to increasingly impassioned peaks on the line “A Message from the stars.” A gentle guitar jangle carries the song forward, lifting some of its emotional weight. A string interlude zigzags through the arrangement as the vocal rises into a high croon, and tension builds until the full force of the performance comes crashing back. Directed and edited by Fabrizio Grasso, with concept and production by Davide Debenedetti for Filmico, the video makes that division visible. October perform on the rink beneath bright backlights, framed against rows of empty seats, while members of Sgularat Hockey Club Milano skate around them in yellow and black. The musicians hold their positions as the players accelerate, compete, and cut across the space between them. Pads, helmets, and sticks give anger and frustration a physical vocabulary; the ice supplies the emotional temperature. There is something both funny and painfully apt about bringing protective equipment into a love song. Here, the action surrounding the band becomes the argument nobody is having aloud: misunderstandings, thwarted attempts at connection, and the helplessness of trying to reach someone who has become difficult to recognise. Grasso lets the rink carry the metaphor, its broad white expanse accommodating all that activity without offering much warmth. Watch the video for Universe below: October formed in Milan in 2024, bringing together musicians whose backgrounds include Grandi Animali Marini, Il Fieno, NOA, and Egokid, alongside collaborations with Veracrash and I Ministri. Villa handles guitar and vocals, joined by bassist Dario Giordano, drummer Paolo Soffientini, and synth player Davide “dEbE” Debenedetti. Their debut was recorded at Casamedusa with Francesco Campanozzi and Frigo Studio with Francesco Ferrari, then mixed and mastered by Paolo Mauri. Released on March 30, 2026, Dancing Like an Idiot is available digitally and on vinyl. Listen to Universe below and order the album here. Dancing like an idiot by OCTOBER Follow October: Facebook Instagram Bandcamp The post “A Message From the Stars” — Milan Art-Rock Quartet October Put Love on Ice in Their Video for “Universe” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.
items._cn_summary: 米兰四人乐队 October 凭借首张专辑《Dancing Like an Idiot》中的第四支单曲《Universe》展开艺术摇滚式的情感叙事。歌曲以灵活的贝斯律动撑起新波 funk 骨架，吉他延音与留白制造出渐进摇滚式的张力拉伸。Gianluca Villa 的高音域演唱融入了 Peter Gabriel 式的克制与爆发力，弦乐间奏在声乐攀升中编织紧张感。MV 由 Fabrizio Grasso 执导，将乐队置于冰球场中央，米兰 Sgularat 曲棍球队员的冲撞滑行隐喻亲密关系中无声的摩擦与隔阂。护具与冰面将情绪外化为可见的对抗，幽默又心酸地揭示了感情中的距离感与表达困境。整体呈现介于后朋克与艺术摇滚之间的成熟质感，融合视觉概念与音乐叙事，但实验性元素相对有限。

items._cn_summary: 这张1975年的萨尔萨专辑以拉丁打击乐为核心，融合铜管、钢琴与人声，形成层次丰富的对话。打击乐手罗贝托·罗埃纳在法尼亚唱片黄金时期推出的这张作品，展现了严谨的编曲结构，同时保留现场演出的临场感与张力。铜管乐句锐利，钢琴俏皮灵动，人声在热情与忧郁之间游走，各声部在精心设计下相互呼应，偶有激烈的碰撞。此次黑胶复刻采用保留原始质感的重制规格，为听众提供接触纽约萨尔萨的契机。整体制作成熟、编排考究，但更多是在传统框架内的精细打磨，缺乏突破性的实验元素。对于世界音乐爱好者而言，是了解拉丁音乐传统的优质入口。

The new edition, titled Exploding In Slow Motion: The Complete Channel The Spirits Recordings 2013-2017CE, features the full original album, which was nominated for the Mercury Prize in 2016. It also takes in their two EPs from the period – Prophecy and Death To The Planet – and four previously unreleased recordings. One of them, One, 'Late Night Party Jam 2', was recorded at London's Total Refreshment Centre, the now-shuttered music venue that the band served as unofficial residents of for a number of years. items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — The band's fourth studio album, second with singer Paul Menel at the microphone--plus they have the enlistment of Noel McCalla (Smallcreep's Day, Acting Very Strange), which excites me. All the names (except Paul's) are familiar to me. A February 1989 release, let's see what they've got for us!1. "War Heroes" (6:26) so what's wrong with Paul Menel's voice!? He sounds like any/every IQ singer--and he's definitely not bad. He holds pitch, he displays an appropriate level of emotional engagement with the lyrics and music. (8.875/10) 2. "Drive On" (4:57) like one of the "B" songs from a 1980s Genesis (or Phil Collins) song, very typical of music in the 1980s. Not bad, just . . . familiar. (8.75/10)3. "Nostalgia" (2:22) the instrumental intro to "Falling Apart ?" is quite Steve Hackett-ish--even down to the basic alternating-two-chord construction. Nice guitar work. Classic NeoProg/Genesis/Hackett bombast. (4.875/5)4. "Falling Apart at the Seams" (7:47) theatric and quite proficient. What are the criticisms of this band and album? This is as high quality NeoProg as I've ever heard (though I am by no means a fan or flaming advocate of the sub-genre). In the context of everything/anything I've ever heard from this band, this stands up there with any/all of it; if you're Genesis/NeoProg fan you've got to love this! Mike Holmes' guitar work and the overall sound palette and mix are quite extraordinary! (13.667/15)5. "Sold On You" (4:40) another typical 1980s offering that sounds like it came from Genesis or Mike + The Mechanics' "All I Need Is a Miracle" only with slightly proggier (and better) instrumental performances. The lyrics are just as cheesy as anything from the era. (8.875/10) 6. "Through My Fingers" (5:30) yes, that's Tony Banks taking on the BLUE NILE sound and style, only, like everybody else on the planet who loves and admires the band, they are unable to slow it down and strip it down to the degree that the Scots do. And we have yet another very solid performance from Paul Menel. (8.875/10)7. "Wurensh" (9:37) a prog-oriented band's obligatory "epic," this one plays out like a 1980s Genesis tune. I mean: exactly! Even the guitar arpeggi and syncopated bass and drum rhythm play is straight out of a Phil-Tony-Mike jam attempt. Granted, this is Paul Menel's weakest vocal performance on the album--partly do to the way his voice is mixed back into the soundscape, partly due to the fact that the band really didn't give him much to bite into. Great guitar work from Mike Holmes in the fifth minute. Plus, it is quite obvious that the band wanted this one to kick into symphonic-Yes-like territory--and they almost do; they just forgot to include/account for the importance of the lyrics, message, and vocal performance. Despite the flaws, I find it interesting to hear so much of Dutch NeoProg band KNIGHT AREA's Under a New Sign in this. Like my disappointment in Wobbler upon finding that their magnificent sound and melodies on 2011's Rites at Dawn had come from (almost directly lifted from) both Yes (Close to the Edge) and Gentle Giant's debut album. (17.5/20)8. "Nothing At All" (4:46) a solid representation of a pop-friendly prog song coming from a prog or even "classic rock" hair band of this era. Nothing to complain or get angry about as it is simply a purely-perfect represent of the popular music of the day. Fine performances all, plodding along as they all did at that time, with the same sound palette and pristine sound engineering of the day that everyone switching into the digital world were producing. (8.75/10) Total Time: 50:52Despite my love of Genesis' two 1976 studio albums (from which all things "NeoProg" came), I really don't know this band very well: though I've listened to pretty much every album they've ever made, I've never really felt "won over" by their achievements. Their sound palette doesn't repel me: it's rather warm and comforting; their vocalists or musicians and soloists always seem proficient and competent, their compositions aren't poor or repulsive. I think they're just . . . okay--very much like a 1980s Genesis song/album: Nice to listen to but nothing that will bring me back--nothing that wow's me as "That's new!" or "That's fresh!" Are You Sitting Comfortably represents, for me, a perfectly fitting and high-quality Genesis-like pop-friendly NeoProg of its day; nothing more and nothing less.B/four stars; a very solid, highly-respectable NeoProg album.
items._cn_summary: 这张1989年的第四张录音室专辑由保罗·梅内尔演唱，新主唱诺埃尔·麦卡拉的加入也受到关注。评论认为多数曲目延续八十年代英国前卫摇滚与创世纪式的写法：旋律清晰、吉他与整体音色表现出色，但部分作品在旋律架构和歌词上较为模式化。长曲《在缝隙中崩塌》和《沃伦什》展示了两人的器乐能力，尤其吉他、贝斯与鼓的交错推进；不过后者的人声被压入配器，歌词与演唱也偏弱，导致宏大感未能完全成立。整体技术成熟，但创新有限。

items.body: EYAA takes its name from a cry of encouragement tied to trance. The French-Ghanaian trio put out “Luku Luku” on Sharma Records on 2 October, the first of five singles leading to their first EP. The voice is Kyekyeku‘s, a singer and guitarist from Accra who now lives in Bayonne, in south-west France, and has worked with highlife veterans Pat Thomas and Ebo Taylor. He formed the seven-piece Ah! Kwantou in 2019, and two of its members, bassist Kevin Bucquet and drummer Fred Faure, are the other two thirds of EYAA. In EYAA, Bucquet plays synths and runs the machines as well as the bass, and he, Faure and Kyekyeku composed “Luku Luku” together, with Kyekyeku writing the words. Kyekyeku sings in Twi, pidgin and English over Faure’s drums and Bucquet’s bass, with synths and machines adding the electronics, and the grooves draw on afro-funk, highlife and afrobeat to make an afro-electro built for dancing. This year the trio has played in France, in Accra at Les Francophonies Festival, and in Portugal at Tom de Festa Festival in Tondela. Listen to “Luku Luku” HERE The post Daily Discovery: LUKU LUKU – EYAA appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items._cn_summary: EYAA是一支法籍-加纳混血三人组合，首张单曲《Luku Luku》以阿克拉歌手Kyekyeku为主唱，结合贝斯手兼合成器操作者Bucquet与鼓手Faure，将加纳传统highlife、afrobeat、afro-funk的律动与现代电子音色相融合，形成专为舞池而作的afro-electro。Kyekyeku此前曾与Pat Thomas、Ebo Taylor等highlife前辈合作，创作中以特威语、皮钦语和英语交替演唱，乐器编制在传统非洲节奏基底上叠加合成器与电子机器。乐队今年已在法国、阿克拉Les Francophonies音乐节及葡萄牙Tom de Festa音乐节演出，展现出跨大西洋音乐对话的独特性。整体定位介于世界音乐与电子舞曲之间，具备文化融合视角，但在实验性与声音设计的前沿突破方面仍偏向传统律动的延伸。

items.body: Virgin Birth, an industrial punk trio from Louisville, Kentucky, will release the six-song EP The Dead End on 16 October 2026 via Never Nervous Records. The band recorded the EP at The Slaughtered Lamb Studio in Louisville. The title track became available on streaming platforms on 2 October 2026, ahead of the full release. Virgin Birth is Phillip Olympia (vocals, synthesizers), Jake Miller (guitar) and Matt Haas (bass). Never Nervous Records described “The Dead End” as continuing the band’s “fascination with the darker corners of electronic music, punk, and the increasingly stupid world we all find ourselves living in.” The label said the band’s earlier releases “looked outward at collapse on a larger scale,” while the new songs are “more immediate, claustrophobic, and personal.” A music video for the title track is set to follow within the week, according to Never Nervous Records. “The Dead End” arrives digitally across major streaming platforms. More live dates and physical releases are planned through Never Nervous Records. About Virgin Birth Virgin Birth formed in Louisville as an industrial synth punk project led by Phillip Olympia and Jake Miller. The duo released its debut EP, “The Forest,” on 26 May 2023 through Never Nervous Records. The nine-track EP included backing vocals from Mandy Keathley and cover art by Albie Mason, and was mixed and mastered by Jake Miller at The Slaughtered Lamb Studio. Virgin Birth followed with the three-song EP “From Behind” on 14 April 2024, also recorded at The Slaughtered Lamb Studio. The band released “I Can’t Read” as a single in March 2025 ahead of its debut full-length album, “Total Annihilation,” issued 2 May 2025 via Never Nervous Records on digital formats and cassette. The ten-track album was again mixed and mastered by Jake Miller at The Slaughtered Lamb Studio, with Olympia handling vocals, synthesizers, drum machines and guitars, and Miller on guitars and synthesizers. Virgin Birth released the remix single “Don’t Tell Me [neu flesh remix]” in August 2025, followed the next month by “SPLIT,” a split release with Scary Black. Matt Haas joined the band on bass by June 2026, when Virgin Birth released a cover of Nirvana’s “Floyd the Barber” as a trio for the first time. “The Dead End” is Virgin Birth’s first EP since “From Behind” in 2024.
items._cn_summary: 这是来自美国肯塔基州路易斯维尔的三人乐队 Virgin Birth 即将发行的六首曲目 EP 资讯，厂牌为独立厂牌 Never Nervous Records。乐队由主唱兼合成器手 Phillip Olympia、吉他手 Jake Miller 和贝斯手 Matt Haas 组成，作品延续了电子音乐与朋克的朋克根源，并被厂牌描述为聚焦于当下世界、以更内省与压迫感的方式呈现。此前乐队已发行多张 EP 与首张全长专辑《Total Annihilation》，录音均出自路易斯维尔的 The Slaughtered Lamb Studio，由 Miller 担任混音与母带。标题曲已于 2026 年 10 月初率先在流媒体上线，音乐录影带也将随后释出。本文为新闻稿性质的发行公告，未涉及实际音乐评论与曲目分析。
